title: Federer tears up during Tennis Hall of Fame induction
text:
An emotional Roger Federer said he was still writing his love letter to the sport that "meant the world" to him as the 20-time Grand Slam champion was inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport, Rhode Island.

Federer, ​who was inducted alongside broadcaster and journalist Mary Carillo, reflected on his storied career in a speech that brought him to tears a few times.

"This is one of the greatest honours of my life," Federer said. "They call this the Hall of Fame, but fame was never the goal.

"My goal was to spend my life doing something ​I love … with people who love ‌it as much as I do."

His opening words, after his introduction speech from his wife Mirka, were: "Oh man. This is very high level and a tough act to follow."

He joked: "I don't know if you have been practising secretly" before praising his wife's presentation of the 274th Hall of Famer.

It began to get tough for him about halfway through, when he talked about his childhood hero, Stefan Edberg, when he said these are "happy tears."

Then he was brought to tears again when he spoke about his longtime coach Severin Luthi, before he wanted to thank Mirka for helping him on his journey.

"Now the Mirka part," he said, pausing before breaking into tears. "Oh gosh, this such a mess."

He tried to joke, but the tears took over like a quick return at the net.

"I need tissues and sunglasses, everything to protect me right now," he told the crowd, fighting back more tears.

The Swiss captured a men's-record eight Wimbledon titles and spent 310 weeks as the world number one. He also won six Australian Open crowns, five US Open titles and one French Open title.

And he did it all while playing with elegance, a signature ‌headband – apparently wearing more than 5,000 of them during his career, he quipped in his address – and almost always two pairs of ⁠socks.

"Tennis meant the world to me. Not just playing, not just winning, but creating something ‌new," said Federer, who retired in 2022 with 103 ​ATP Tour titles.

"It's a mentality I have. ‌I used to play serve and volley, I had a transition game, I played way beyond the baseline sometimes, or on top of the baseline.

"And I would even try to sneak up on my opponents on my return, and some call it the SABR [Sneak Attack by Roger] today.

"This is what was important to me on the court, but so much of what ​was ‌really important happened off the court."

The 45-year-old got emotional while thanking his coaches, doctors and family, including wife Mirka, who praised Federer for his character off the court as husband, father and friend.

As his name entered the Hall of Fame, Federer ⁠said he was proud that Switzerland was coming with him, recalling how ‌he loved watching tennis as a 13-year-old ‌ball boy in Basel.

"I'm still writing my love letter to tennis, and my time as a player is done, but tennis will always stand ‌at the intersection of everything I care most about," he said.

"My family, our friendships, the past 40 years, the future we're building – tennis, for me, is responsible for it all. So this is not a goodbye."

The ‌Swiss said he ​was "incredibly lucky" to have played ⁠with different generations of tennis players, from Andre Agassi and Lleyton Hewitt to Andy Roddick, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic.

But he added that his induction was not only an opportunity to look back on his career, but also ahead to the future of the game.

"We all leave the court eventually, but the sport keeps evolving," Federer said.

"And as the ⁠pace of professional tennis speeds up, as the sport becomes even more global, I so hope it will keep some of that amateur spirit. Keep the camaraderie among the ‌players.

"I hope the players ‌will stay young at heart and stay true to their authentic selves, and always remember, never stop ​asking questions or taking risks.

"Do things with the game we've never seen before. Keep pushing this sport we love to the next level and keep getting better, better, and better."

Billie Jean King (left) introduced Mary Carillo for her induction to the International Tennis Hall of Fame. (Getty Images: ITHF/Clive Brunskill)

Carillo, inducted as a contributor, is a member of the Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame.

King said: "She has earned her spot in sports journalism and she has earned her spot in Newport."

Reuters/AP

title: Nearly 400 trees face chop for new $96m MotoGP street circuit
text:
Nearly 400 trees will be removed in Adelaide's eastern parklands to make way for a new MotoGP street circuit costing $96 million, the South Australian government has revealed.

Premier Peter Malinauskas has unveiled the design for a 4.13 kilometre-long circuit that is set to host MotoGP from November 2027.

The Tour Down Under would also race on the track from January 2028, the government announced.

The circuit redesign would see 42 significant trees felled, along with a further 335 of what the government has categorised as "regulated, unregulated, invasive, dead or poor health" trees.

A further 88 trees would be relocated while another 22 were "under investigation", the premier said.

Premier Peter Malinauskas has unveiled the design for the circuit set to host MotoGP. (Carl Saville: ABC News)

Of the 22 trees under investigation, the premier said 15 were significant trees.

Mr Malinauskas said trees would be replaced on a 10 to 1 basis, meaning 3,770 trees would be planted.

The government would also procure a new temporary pit building, rather than a permanent building.

The premier said there had been some "conjecture" about a permanent building but admitted the government "did look at the options".

Prior to the release of the plans, there had been protests about tree loss, with more than 43,000 people signing a petition calling for a halt to works.

The proposed Adelaide Circuit Redevelopment design. (Supplied)

"I don't think this will stop the protests, I mean, people are entitled to protest against it regardless," Mr Malinauskas said.

"But what it does do is makes it very clear that this government is committed to investing in our parklands."

The bulk of the trees would be removed between Wakefield and Bartels Road.

Public consultation on the track will start on Monday and run until September 20.

A map showing the planned circuit. (Supplied: SA Government)

Mr Malinauskas said the government was "genuinely interested in the feedback it will receive".

The new track would have 15 turns — up from 14 currently — and a 900-metre long straight along Dequetteville Terrace.

Top speeds for the MotoGP would be 343km/h while the Supercars would reach up to 265km/h, the government said.

It was also forecasting a $200 million a year economic benefit.

title: Former White House teleprompter operator fined over insider trading
text:
A former White House teleprompter operator accused of using inside knowledge to make bets on the prediction market Kalshi has been ordered to turn over more than $US100,000 in profits and pay a $US65,000 fine as part of a settlement with federal authorities.

The settlement with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, announced Friday local time, also dealt Gabriel Perez a three-year trading ban.

Mr Perez was placed on unpaid leave from his job at the White House after reports emerged that he used his position to make bets on what US President Donald Trump would say in speeches.

Trump teleprompter operator suspended US President Donald Trump's longtime technician allegedly made over $142,000 by placing bets on what Donald Trump would say in speeches.

The White House did not immediately comment on the settlement.

A White House official said in July that Mr Perez was no longer in his position but did not say if he had been fired or resigned.

The commission found that Mr Perez made $US107,500 ($150,080) on prediction markets by betting on words and phrases that would appear in Mr Trump's speeches between December 2025 and February 2026.

"In his position, Perez had access to presidential speeches prior to those speeches being delivered and Perez misappropriated that information, in breach of his duty of trust and confidence," according to a release from the commission.

Mr Perez was ordered to repay his profits in full, along with the $US65,000 ($90,746) civil penalty, which the commission said was a reduction because of his "exemplary cooperation".

As details emerged on July 16, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said it was "unfortunate" and "a disgrace".

AP

title: Scott turns back clock in Tour Championship title tilt
text:
A much-craved second major continues to elude him but Adam Scott may be one great round from capping his decorated career with a second season-ending Tour Championship title.

As golf's biggest names jostle for the $US10 million ($A14 million) winner's cheque in Atlanta, Scott quietly but steadily climbed into a tie for third place entering the final round.

The 2006 champion compiled a classy third-round five-under-par 65 at Atlanta's East Lake Golf Club to position himself three shots behind Norwegian leader Viktor Hovland.

With his own 65, Hovland turned a halfway share of the lead into a one-shot buffer over American Ryan Gerard (66) as he reached 15 under.

So often cruelling his winning chances on the greens, putting was for once Scott's saving grace on Saturday (Sunday AEST).

The former world No.1 drained 132 yards worth of putts, including near 25-footers for three of his six birdies on the eighth, 13th and 17th holes.

It was Scott's second-best putting round of the year and presented the 2013 Masters champion with an enticing opportunity to land first PGA Tour victory since February 2020.

"It's a good spot," Scott said.

"Within striking distance. It's so congested, though. It's going to need a really great round, I think. There's someone lurking who's going to have that."

Min Woo Lee, Australia's only other player in the elite 30-man field for the $US40 million showpiece, remains an outside hope of becoming the first Tour Championship debutant to win since Xander Schauffele in 2017.

Lee is equal ninth after carding a third-round 66, but will need to reel in a raft of superstars.

At 12 under, world No.1 Scottie Scheffler (66) shares third spot with fellow American Chris Gotterup (67), Scott and Swede Ludvig Aberg (65).

Rory McIlroy was the biggest mover of the day, a round of 63 vaulting the world No.2 from 23rd to joint seventh with Cameron Young (68) at 10 under.

Then it's Lee and American trio Russell Henley (66), Jacob Bridgeman (66) and Sam Burns (67) all at nine under.

The 46-year-old Scott is relishing his crack at another big title.

"I can kind of stick with my game plan of being fairly conservative at least for the front nine," Scott said.

"And if I can execute that, then maybe I've got to start flag hunting a little bit and being a bit more aggressive than I have been.

"But I'll try to play that by ear when I'm out there. It's fun to be in the mix for the Tour Championship and the FedExCup."

AAP

title: Socceroo Volpato scores long-range goal in Serie A win
text:
A long-range strike from Socceroo Cristian Volpato has helped his Italian side Sassuolo claim a 2-1 win over Torino in its Serie A clash.

With the match scoreless through the opening half hour, Sassuolo counterattacked from its own half in the 32nd minute.

The ball came to Socceroo Volpato, who ripped a shot from well outside the penalty box.

The low strike curled and beat Torino goalkeeper Diego Mascardi to break the deadlock.

Torino levelled the score at the end of the first half, but Domenico Berardi's 78th-minute winner secured Sassuolo its first win of this league campaign.

Elsewhere, fellow Socceroo Mohamed Toure scored a double in Norwich City's 4-1 win over Burnley in the English Championship.

He has now scored 11 goals from 14 Championship matches since making his first appearance in the league in February.

Twenty-year-old Socceroo Paul Okon-Engstler made his debut in Germany's top flight for club Köln.

Okon-Engstler played 65 minutes as Köln defeated Hoffenheim 3-2 in the opening round of the Bundesliga season.

title: 'I will always be walking in the desert': Birdsville ranger hangs up uniform after 30 years
text:
Don Rowlands is the keeper of Central Australia's vast Simpson Desert.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this story contains images of people who have died.

When he closes his eyes, the wind gives way to older sounds, of feet dancing in the sand, as the echoes of his ancestors carry across the "big sandhill country" they know as Munga-Thirri.





The Wangkangurru occupied the Simpson Desert for tens of thousands of years. (Supplied: Don Rowlands) For most people, the Simpson Desert is a bucket-list wilderness to pass through, but for Don, it's home: the traditional lands of the Wangkangurru Yarluyandi people.

For more than three decades, he has been the ranger in charge of Munga-Thirri National Park, Queensland's largest protected area near Birdsville in the state's far south-west corner.

Being Birdsville's ranger is a role he has defined. Each day is a delicate balance of managing conservation, visitor access and preserving culture.

Don Rowlands has an Order of Australia Medal (OAM) for his services to the community and the environment. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

But the time has come for the lone ranger to hang up his uniform.

"The uniform was why I get up in the morning. I'm so proud of the uniform and what it represents to Queensland; it's the ultimate for me," he says.

"Despite having to move on, my heart is still in the desert and it's my traditional lands and I have a responsibility to care for it and I will.

"No matter where the path takes me, I will always be walking in the desert."

Don Rowlands is retiring as ranger in charge of Munga-Thirri National Park. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

Freedom and identity

Queensland's slice of the 1 million hectares of the Simpson Desert's sand dunes, this year awash with floodwater and wildflowers, was gazetted as a national park in 1967.

Part of Don Rowlands's job is testing tracks and ensuring access for tourists in the desert. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

A lot has changed in the desert since; much of the bush tucker Don found as a kid is gone and birds have thinned out.

Feral animals such as cats continue to wreak havoc, and early on it was millions of rabbits.

"When the calicivirus came along in 1996 and wiped them out that was a big thing for me," Don says.

When Don became the first Queensland Parks and Wildlife ranger employed to care for Munga-Thirri National Park in 1994, he quickly set about reshaping its future.

In drought or flood, Don Rowlands says the desert is always somewhere he wants to be. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

He pushed for the park to be recognised by its traditional name and became a leading advocate for native title recognition, a fight that took two decades, culminating in a determination in 2014.

The work placed him in a space he knew well, navigating the ground between two worlds.

"Most of my mob were so entrenched with growing up with white people that they didn't want to upset them," Don says.

"I did a lot of the work by myself."

The Rowland family has a shed displaying artefacts and local history. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

Growing up in Birdsville as a ward of the state, Don's earlier life was dictated by government authorities and police.

" That hurt as kids and we realised that we had another boss, someone else who had control of our lives and that took a bit for us to adjust. "

The quiet routine of putting on his ranger uniform every day for the past 32 years marked a shift in Don.

Don Rowlands lives with his wife of 52 years, Lyn Rowlands. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

"It's given me the freedom to talk about my heritage, to talk about my people in the desert," he says.

"It gave you identity; you're identified with a group of people who care for native animals, for the landscape.





Don Rowlands spent much of his life in the saddle as a ringer working in mustering camps. (Supplied: Don Rowlands) "The uniform is what set me apart from my past life."

Constant in community

No-one knows the desert like Don; he can distinguish every dune and reads the shifting sands like a well-worn map.

He has been involved in dozens of rescues, many of those alongside Stephan Pursell, who was Birdsville's police officer for almost a decade.

Stephan Pursell and Don Rowlands enjoying a cuppa out the back of the Rowlands's cafe. (Supplied: Don Rowlands)

"He always joked that he could actually now sit up in the front of the police car rather than in the back," Stephan says.

" Without Don, the rescues and just general travel would have been near impossible for me. "

Beyond working together, the pair became mates.

"I don't think he's replaceable to be honest," Stephan says.

Don Rowlands has great relationships with police officers who are stationed in Birdsville. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

At the Birdsville Hotel, Ben Fullagher says Don's retirement is going to leave a huge gap in the community.

"We call on Don usually around conditions in the desert, what the creeks are doing, what the floodwaters over the summer might be doing," he says.

"It's a very important part of the local economy, ensuring access is open and regular for the tourism across the desert."

All for family

It is a lifetime of knowledge Don has shared with anyone who comes seeking it.

He hopes the next ranger will too.

Dreamtime and creation stories were how Indigenous people memorised the landscape. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

Don has followed and researched his people's songlines through the desert, the pathways that connect places, people and stories.

"I'm the only one that knows where they are," he says.

The reason behind everything for Don is family.

Some of Don Rowlands's great-grandkids who live in Birdsville. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

"That's one of my aims, to make sure my family don't disappear off the map," he says.

"It's all about preserving our story … it's really important that I leave my message here for my kids."

Through every success and setback, his greatest support has been his wife, Lyn Rowlands.

"I was really proud of him to be wearing that uniform … that he had a job in government after the way he was treated."

Lyn Rowlands has run a cafe in Birdsville for six years, beside the house she grew up in. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh)

There have been times when Lyn has worked as a ranger too, along with their daughter, Peta Rowlands.

"I was very young at the time … it hasn't been until a lot later in life that I've sort of appreciated what the job has meant not just for me, his daughter, for him and our family but more for our culture," Peta says.

" I don't think he realises how deeply people care for him and appreciate him and what he's done. "





Don Rowlands wants to keep sharing Aboriginal stories. (ABC Western Qld: Hannah Walsh) He may be hanging up the uniform but the work for Don is far from over.

"I don't want to stay at home and just do nothing. I'm toying with a few touring ideas, tag along and go off into some of this wild country," he says.

"I want to talk about the bad times and the good times but the fight I've had in the middle to not erase the bad times but improve the good.

"You can have a voice, and people should have a voice. For too long we didn't have a voice."

title: Superfan shares fragile X message with ABC newsrooms across Australia
text:
For Newcastle local Hayden Eastbury, the ABC is not just something he tunes into each morning, noon, and night

It is a passion that has taken him and his family across the country.

The ABC first learned of the Eastbury family's endeavour to visit every bureau in October last year, when Hayden met one of his favourite presenters, Nate Byrne, at the Perth Royal Show.

Hayden, who lives with fragile X syndrome, has since ticked off 36 bureaus, more than half of the ABC's 56 locations around Australia.

When he and his family set off from their New South Wales home, the goal was to visit as many ABC studios as they could to honour Hayden's lifelong passion for the public broadcaster.

Hayden has met presenters from across Australia while travelling with his family, a journey that has taken just under two years. (Supplied: Phil Eastbury)

"Travelling around Australia, a lot of people can find a bit of a theme, you know, visit national parks, or see the 'big things'. But our theme has been finding purpose for Hayden through the ABC," dad Phil Eastbury told the ABC.

"We also kind of felt as a family a bit 'therapy-ed' out, if I'm honest, so we thought what better way to seek new opportunities, and develop a lot of what we learnt through therapy, we can take it out on the road and apply that out in the community."

The Eastbury family say they are determined to reach every ABC bureau in Australia, regardless of how remote the location is. (Supplied: Phil Eastbury)

Phil said the visits have helped Hayden, who one day hopes to work for the public broadcaster, develop his confidence in asking and answering questions.

"He has learnt how to hold the microphone, how to ask probing questions; it has really helped to develop his inquisitive nature," he said.

Hayden met Leigh Sales, who presents shows such as Australian Story and The Assembly, where she mentors autistic journalism students. (Supplied: Phil Eastbury)

A birthday present from the ABC

This week marks another special milestone for Hayden: his 18th birthday.

To celebrate, his favourite presenters from across the country, many of whom he watches every day, have wished him happy birthday.

Loading...

When asked what bureau was his favourite, Hayden said there was a clear winner.

"My favourite bureau I've loved, I think, is Perth because it's a good one," Hayden said.

"I loved Pamela [Medlen] and using her desk, and Tabarak Al Jrood's weather wall."

Hayden shows how everyone is unique

Fragile X is a mutation of the X chromosome that can lead to a wide range of physical, intellectual and behavioural symptoms, according to the Fragile X Association of Australia.

Executive director Wendy Bruce said Hayden's story had resonated with so many as an example of how families with children with disabilities can find original ways to fulfil their children's passion.

"I think it has helped to deepen people's understanding that everyone with a disability is unique; they all have different strengths, abilities, challenges, and that leads to needing different support needs," Ms Bruce said.

The Kalgoorlie ABC team in Western Australia gave Hayden the chance to be their radio presenter. (Supplied: Phil Eastbury)

"Their interactions with so many people around the country have really painted a broader picture of living with fragile X syndrome and disability, but [also] the possibilities of being so engaged in the community."

Ms Bruce said it had inspired other families to take "the road less travelled".

Hayden was able to meet up with ABC News presenter Joe O'Brien while in Sydney. (Supplied: Phil Eastbury)

title: Aussie qualifer completes rare grand slam feat
text:
There is a very good reason why facing big-hitting French Open and Wimbledon semifinalist Marta Kostyuk in the US Open first round holds no fears for late-blooming Australian trailblazer Storm Hunter.

The 32-year-old has just sent tennis officials scrambling through the record books after qualifying for the Open's main draw for the first time.

Historians could only confirm Hunter is the first active Australian player to successfully qualify for all four grand slams, a rare feat few others from anywhere have accomplished.

De Minaur gets qualifier in US Open first round Alex de Minaur appears to have a kind draw for the year's final grand slam, but Australia's perennial hope will face a precociously formidable obstacle if he wants to make it to the quarterfinals for the third straight year.

Hunter did not do it easily, taking out compatriot and great mate Maddison Inglis in her first match, fending off two match points in her second and waiting through a 24-hour weather delay to advance with a third straight sudden-death victory.

"This is the last slam on my list to tick off to get through qualies and coming in I hadn't played many singles matches in the last few months so, yeah, it feels amazing," Hunter said.

Having missed more than a year after rupturing an Achilles tendon, Hunter is back in the Flushing Meadows main draw for a first time since 2023.

Her "reward" is a first-round tussle on day one with the 11th-seeded Kostyuk, who is coming off charges to the last four at both Roland Garros and the All England Club.

"Yeah, it's tough," said the one-time world number one doubles ace.

"She's obviously having a really good year. She's a great player, very physical with the way she plays and a really good competitor.

"So it's going to be tough. Obviously a very quick turnaround from playing qualifiers to my first round tomorrow, but I'm feeling good and she's the one who's under all the pressure to play against me and I have practised with her before.

"I know what her level is and I know it's going to be a challenge, but I'm up for a challenge. It's going to be fun. I'm going to enjoy it.

"There's been lots of times in my career I didn't think I'd be back playing at this level, so to be back in the main draw of a slam is awesome, and I'm just going to go out and enjoy it and give it a good crack."

Hunter is among six Australians playing on Monday.

Kim Birrell faces Petra Marcinko, Talia Gibson also plays a Croatian in veteran Donna Vekic and fellow rising star Taylah Preston takes on American Alycia Parks.

Adam Walton, up against China's Yibing Wu, and Aleksandar Vukic playing Japan's Rei Sakamoto are the only Aussie men in first-round action.

Sixth seed Alex de Minaur opens his campaign on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST).

AAP

title: 'I've got enough to live on': The 80-year-old giving away his harvest
text:
A humble pumpkin patch in the Whitsundays is feeding far more than stomachs.

Retired canegrower Darcy Emmerson grows the pumpkins in the foothills of a coastal mountain range at Kelsey Creek, 14 kilometres south-west of Proserpine.

Twice a week he donates about a tonne of pumpkins to community groups, charities, churches, daycare centres, doctors' surgeries and businesses in Proserpine, Cannonvale and Airlie Beach.

Proserpine library assistant Libby Crisp and Darcy Emmerson. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

Each delivery the 80-year-old makes comes with the expectation of nothing in return.

"It's not actually a charity run, but it's a little gift for people," Mr Emmerson said.

Delivery day

It's overcast, and there's a light drizzle of rain when he sets out, the two-way radio in his old ute alive with chatter from harvesters and haul-out drivers.

He stops at Meals on Wheels where he's warmly met by volunteers.

Meals on Wheels kitchen volunteers Cathy O'Keefe and Leanne Alexander will use Darcy's pumpkins in meals for the community. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

"I try and get them big ones, so they can cut the whole thing up. That way it goes a bit further," he said.

"The Pumpkin Man", as he is affectionately known, is greeted with a hug at the Proserpine Community Centre.

Proserpine Community Centre community support officer Ashley Gunn thanks Darcy Emmerson. (ABC Tropica North: Aimee Mitchell)

Support officer Ashley Gunn wheels out a large timber trolley, made by the local men's shed, and it's soon overflowing.

"We have people come in just for pumpkins," Ms Gunn said.

"People of all ages. A lot of them will take a pumpkin on their way out and then come back with extra produce that they've got out of their garden.

"It's sort of like a give-and-take system, and there's no judgement."

Darcy's ute full of pumpkins is a welcome sight at the Proserpine Community Centre. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

Generosity

Mr Emmerson asks for no money, saying he doesn't need it.

"I've got enough to live on," he said.

"I just feel like I've got to help, you know? Help people. That's what this should be all about, shouldn't it?"

He becomes emotional when talking about what the community has taught him.

"I didn't realise … there's so many disabled people around. I didn't realise how many," he said through tears.

"When I stuck my head into that respite centre one day, I couldn't believe it. It was chock-a-block. I'm gonna get a tear in my eye every time I go there."

Community inspiration

Darcy Emmerson grows bugle, butternut and kent varieties of pumpkins. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

Mr Emmerson's generosity has also inspired others.

A local sign-writer has professionally created a sign for the pumpkin stand under his letterbox after seeing the 80-year-old's handwritten version.

An anonymous donor gave him a net for the back of his ute to stop the pumpkins falling out.

He still doesn't know who left it.

"Oh, I appreciate it. Yeah, that's for sure."

Darcy Emmerson's generosity has inspired others to give back in his community. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

A restaurant has added "Darcy's Pumpkin Soup" to the menu and a local mother, Leah Warren, is writing a children's book inspired by his generosity.

"The generosity really touched me, and it is a value I'd like to instil in my family, and I just thought it was a message that needed to be heard," Ms Warren said.

"If it is made with love and shared with kindness, it is like planting a little pumpkin seed. That kindness then gets shared multiple times over."

Leah Warren is writing a book inspired by the generous pumpkin deliveries. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

The final stop

Mr Emmerson's favourite — and last — stop is the Endeavour Foundation in Cannonvale.

Support worker Julie Harrison says the pumpkins are used by people attending the learning and lifestyle hub.

"We're growing all our own herbs and tomatoes. We bring it in from the garden and incorporate it into our lunch," she said.

Charlie Bell, Jenny Atkinson and Cathy Brown are some of the friendly faces at the Cannonvale Endeavour Foundation Learning and Lifestyle Hub who greet Darcy (far right) each week. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

But just when the delivery run is finished The Pumpkin Man has one more suggestion. "You wouldn't have time to go out to the farm, would you?"

After crossing Goorganga Creek he arrives at the farm his grandparents started in 1918.

"This is Walga. Walga is the Aboriginal name for … kangaroo blood or Aboriginal meeting place," he said while driving past the old family home, through cane paddocks to the pumpkin patch.

The Emmerson family were one of the earliest pioneers of the Proserpine region. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

Hundreds of pumpkins cover the soil mounds. Bugle, butternut and kent varieties are grown in "mud" left over from sugarcane processing at the local mill.

Mr Emmerson is unsure how many are still in the paddock.

"Couldn't even guess. A couple of thousand?"

The pumpkins grow between the cane paddocks. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

As the pumpkin season comes to an end, he says there'll be more pumpkins next year to feed the community.

Along with the help of his 86-year-old mate, other friends and family, he says they'll keep picking the pumpkins.

And when he can no longer make the deliveries himself, he already knows who will take over.

"That's OK. Craig [my son] will do it."

title: Paralympian fell in love with his wife in a traffic jam
text:
When big wave surfer and Paralympic cyclist Matt Formston was writing a list of the traits he desired in a partner, he realised he wasn't half of the things he expected of someone else. So he began working on himself, and eventually found his way to now-wife Rebecca, aka Bex.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

Matt: I had a successful business and sporting career.

It all looked nice, but I wasn't really happy. I'd had a bunch of failed relationships.

It's easy to blame the other person but I realised I needed to take accountability.

I wrote at list of 12 things I'd like in a wife and realised I wasn't at least six of them.

I needed to build a version of me that had those things so I could reasonably expect them of someone else.

That was 2008 and by 2010 I got my first executive job, started riding for Australia. Sounds like a lucky year but there was nothing lucky about it.

The luckiest thing was I met Bex.

Bex: We met online, which was quite pioneering for the time. Really unromantic story.

I'd moved from the UK and had been in Sydney for a couple of months and was trying to meet new people.

We agreed to meet at the beach. I knew he was blind, but I didn't really know how blind.

I got to the beach and just sat down. It was quite busy.

He rang and said, "Where are you?" I said, "Just to the right of the stairs wearing a blue hoodie".

Somehow, he found me.

Matt: I just wandered around looking awkward around people until I guessed it was Bex.

Bex: We went for lunch and I said, "Here's the menu" and he said, "I can't read it".

That was awkward.

A two-for-one deal

Matt and Bex on their wedding day. (Supplied)

Matt: From there we started hanging out every weekend.

We took a camping trip a month later and my parents, who lived nearby, turned up with the whole family.

I remember Bex just being OK with it all. She didn't baulk at it. That was a big tick for me.

On the way home we got stuck in a traffic jam and she just chatted and didn't complain. I fell in love with her in that traffic jam.

Bex: Meeting Matt and being in Sydney was all very exciting and new.

I really liked Matt's passion for where he lives. He's a proud Aussie.

I fell in love with Sydney while falling in love with him. A two-for-one deal.

Getting through tough times

Bex: When having our first baby, he was born right in the middle of a full-on training campaign for Matt for the Paralympics.

I knew that was going to happen but didn't really think it through. I was only 26 and had no family here.

Suddenly I had this newborn and my husband is on his bike for the whole of his paternity leave.

And when he was only eight weeks old, Matt went to Mexico for a couple of weeks.

That was a lot.

Matt is a four-time Para Surfing World Champion. (Supplied)

Matt: That trip I did when our eldest was eight weeks old, I set a world record on that trip.

When my legs wouldn't go and I couldn't breathe, I just thought about Bex at home with the baby without me and no-one was beating me.

Similar happened with our other two kids.

In 2016 when our daughter was born, I was on an Olympic campaign.

Our other son was born in 2018 and I'd booked a filming trip to Indonesia and didn't even have phone coverage.

It's been hard on our relationship.

Teammates in life

Matt and Bex with their three children. (Supplied)

Matt: I've got a list of achievements that fill up more than a couple of pages, but I didn't have any of them until I met Bex.

She's my bedrock. She's allowed me to do all the things I'm able. And she doesn't get any credit for those, but she should.

I've got teams everywhere, but my best teammate is my wife.

Bex: Life with Matt is busy. Exciting. There are always different things going on.

But the relationship is safe and reliable. Even though he's crazy, I trust him.

I can't imagine my life anywhere else.

title: Addisu Gobena wins the 2026 Sydney Marathon, as 40K runners take part
text:
Ethiopian athlete Addisu Gobena has won the 2026 Sydney Marathon, with a record number of runners from across the globe competing.

The first tranche of 40,000 runners hit the pavement at 6:15am to tackle the picturesque 42.2-kilometre route from North Sydney to the Opera House.

It is the second year the marathon is operating under an Abbott World Marathon Major status, seeing competitive marathoners from across the globe run alongside members of the public.

Addisu Gobena has won the 2026 Sydney Marathon, setting a new record. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

Gobena took first place with a record-breaking time of 2:04:42, shaving off more than 1 minute from 2025 Sydney Marathon winner Hailemaryam Kiros's time of 2:06:06.

Returning to Sydney after finishing in second place at last year's event, Gobena ran the fastest marathon ever completed by a male athlete in Australia.

Silver went to Chimdessa Debele Gudeta and Tebello Ramakongoana took third place, with both finishing inside the previous race record.

Kenyan runner Peres Jepchirchir has claimed the women's title, completing the course in 2:18:31.

Peres Jepchirchir has won gold for the women's category. (AAP Image: Nadir Kinani)

The reigning world champion won the event by 3 minutes and 40 seconds, with Irine Cheptai taking second place and Shure Demise Ware finishing in third.

Jepchirchir's time was just shy of the record set by last year's women's winner Sifan Hassan, who ran the course in 02:18:22.

Wheelchair marathoners were the first to cross the finish line on Sunday morning, with the USA's Daniel Romanchuk finishing with a time of 1:26:50, breaking the record of 1:27:15 set by Marcel Hug last year.

Wheelchair athlete Daniel Romanchuk was the first to cross the finish line. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

Paralympic athlete Manuela Schär was the first female to finish with a time of 1:42:04, also setting a new record.

Her winning time took 2 minutes and 48 seconds off Susannah Scaroni's course record of 1:44:52.

Schär is the first athlete to win on all eight Abbott World Marathon Majors courses.

Manuela Schär took gold for the women's wheelchair athletes. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

Andy Buchanan was the first Australian to cross the finish line, completing the course in 2:10:14.

Australia's first woman to finish the marathon., Ellie Pashley, recorded a time of 2:28:28.

Guinness World Record set

Five Dock's Toby Fuller set a record of a different kind, becoming the fastest chemotherapy patient to complete a marathon, as recognised by the Guinness World Records.

When he was 23 years old, Fuller was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that currently has no cure.

Toby Fuller set a Guinness World Records title for being the fastest chemotherapy patient to complete a marathon. (ABC News)

Fuller completed the course in 3 hours and 18 minutes, saying crossing the finish line was "really emotional".

"I'm stoked," he said.

"It's not the time I wanted but I gave it my best.

"I don't get the runner's high, every [kilometre] was hard."

Fuller said he looked forward to celebrating his achievement over a curry with loved ones.

More than $14 million has been raised for charity as part of the event.

title: 'Once in a lifetime': Schoolteacher wins AFL Fantasy competition
text:
Tyler Wagner could hardly watch as the outcome of this year's AFL Fantasy competition came down to the wire.

In the 13 years the Fremantle Dockers diehard had been playing the online game, he never envisioned he would make it here.

With less than a minute to go, Wagner's fantasy team, named Wagmantle, was in the lead by just three fantasy points.

If the opposing team, The Powerhouse, recorded a single stat, the 2026 title was theirs.

As the ball approached Powerhouse's Jarman Impey, the seconds were ticking down, and Wagner could not bear to watch.

Tyler Wagner's Wagmantle managed to beat a number of other fantasy players. (Supplied: Tyler Wagner)

But when he did finally look back up, Impey had dropped the mark.

"It was still nerve-racking because the siren had gone, but sometimes the AFL do late stat corrections," Wagner said.

"My mates went absolutely mental and it was a very, very cool moment.

"But I was still sitting there pacing the hallway just hoping there was no stat correction."

Thirteen years in the making

AFL Fantasy allows users to coach a virtual team of players, who score points based on their real-life performances, using an allocated budget.

Each year approximately 140,000 Australians compete to crown one winner.

This year, the prize on offer was $20,000, two tickets to the AFL Grand Final and a car.

Tyler Wagner is footy obsessed and spends most of his free time either watching or playing. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

Wagner, a 28-year-old PE teacher from South Australia's Riverland, described his win as "overwhelming".

The A-grade footballer had been playing AFL Fantasy since 2014 when he was a teenager.

"I've had a lot of messages from friends and family, which has been really awesome," he said.

"There's a group of year four, fives and sixes that I teach that follow it pretty closely.

"They were ripping me some weeks where I dropped a few in ranks and then they'd give me a kudos when it went up, but those last couple of weeks, they were pretty excited."

Long-suffering Fremantle fans dare to dream

What started as a bit of fun has now given Wagner the opportunity to live out his childhood dream alongside his father.

Fremantle has never won a premiership in its 32-year history and has only once made it to the big dance in 2013.

"My old man has been a Docker supporter since 1995," he said.

Tyler Wagner (right) never had any choice in which team he supported, following in the footsteps of his dad (centre). (Supplied: Tyler Wagner)

"I reckon he might have been the bloody first Fremantle fan in SA.

" It's a no-brainer — if Freo manage to make it, I'm definitely taking dad. "

Wagner is hoping the Dockers, who finished 2026 as minor premiers, can go one better than 2013 and make history.

"I'm definitely a self-confessed Dockers nuffy," he said.

Luke Jackson is Tyler Wagner's favourite player and was a key piece for his fantasy team. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

" To see that would be absolutely everything, especially alongside my dad. "

Luck or strategy?

AFL Fantasy expert Ryan "Heff" Gerlach has been playing fantasy football since 2004, back when it was called Dream Team.

He has since made a career out of the hobby, running a successful podcast known as The Keeper League.

"Winning the competition against 140,000 people is lucky in itself," Gerlach said.

"To do it in a year where there's a good chance of your team playing in the Grand Final, I don't think it could have worked out any better for Tyler."

Ryan "Heff" Gerlach is well known within the growing fantasy football community. (Supplied: Ryan Gerlach)

The statistical side of fantasy sports, mixed with a sense of gaming is what Gerlach said made it such an appealing pastime.

He said while anyone in a position to beat out more than 140,000 people had to be knowledgeable, luck was bound to play some role.

"If I was going to give it a number, I'd say [it's] probably 60 per cent strategy, 40 per cent luck," Gerlach said.

"But you talk to different people and that answer will differ."

Despite the temptation to attribute his once-in-a-lifetime season to skill, Wagner remained humble in his assessment.

"I didn't think that I would even be in the top ten this year, let alone winning the thing," he said.

"In other years I've probably felt like I've put the same amount of effort in, but it just hasn't fallen my way.

"There's definitely a lot of luck involved, but you still need to know your stuff."

title: Victorian roads 'not good enough', premier says amid pothole pledge
text:
The Victorian government is promising to double the number of potholes it fixes on the state's roads this year.

The Carroll government is pledging to fix 500,000 potholes by the end of January, up from 250,000 it previously committed to fixing.

The plan will cost $352 million, on top of more than $1 billion dollars already budgeted for road maintenance.

The issue is becoming a significant election issue, particularly for regional Victorians.

Some regional Victorians have complained they've had to spend registration rebates on fixing tyre damage caused by potholes.

The government says fixing the extra 250,000 potholes will cost $352 million. (Supplied)

Earlier this month, dozens of cars were forced off the road after hitting large potholes that opened up along the Princes Freeway at Bunyip in Victoria's east.

Premier Ben Carroll said the additional spending was justified given the extent of the problem.

"This is absolutely where Victorians want to see their money spent — it is my priority," he said.

"The condition of our roads is not good enough.

"I respect your money and I have made commonsense decisions to show how we can afford it."

Ben Carroll says the state of Victoria's roads is "not good enough". (ABC News)

The government said the extra spending will be partly funded by delaying the completion of three level crossing removals — at Highett Rd and Wickham Rd in Highett and Latrobe St in Mentone — by one year

The government said the work will commence over the coming weeks, as rain reduces and will continue into early next year.

Road crews will target key arterial roads across the state — including the Geelong Ring Road, Western Highway, Calder Highway and Princes Highway — plus regional roads.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson last month announced her party would spend $5 billion over four years on road maintenance if elected.

Shadow Roads Minister Danny O'Brien described the Labor announcement as "a con job".

"Ben Carroll was Roads minister when $214 million was cut from road maintenance over two years," he said.

"Now on the eve of an election, he expects Victorians to believe he will fix the roads, after 12 years of ignoring them?

"Labor has never fixed more than 200,000 potholes in a year and now wants us to believe they'll fix half a million in six months? Spare me."

title: Like it or lump it, the AFL’s wildcard finals are here to stay

Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 Like it or lump it, the AFL’s wildcard finals are here to stay Michael Gleeson August 30, 2026 — 2:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The numbers will tell you wildcard weekend was a roaring success. For the AFL that is all that matters. The league’s case for the wildcard round is a business one. As a business case, it was a phenomenal success. As a sporting case, where integrity, fairness and finding the best teams remain important – flimsy imperatives in a competition with a fixture where compromise is the rule, not the exception – the justification remains doubtful. Bulldogs players celebrate after Tim Membrey missed an after-siren kick that would have put Collingwood into an elimination final. AFL Photos via Getty Images As a case of theatre, the wildcard was box-office drama and the most compelling argument the AFL could have hoped for.

The numbers will say that on both nights the footy was the third-top program viewed nationally after channels Seven and Nine’s news bulletins. About one million people watched on Friday night – 800,000 on free to air TV, another 166,000 streaming and an untold number watching on Foxtel (untold that is because they won’t tell us. Fox is cagey about these things). Loading On Saturday night, there were 720,000 watching free on TV and another 153,000 streaming. On Friday night more than 81,000 people were at the MCG; on Saturday night 91,000 squeezed in.

Advertisement

In recent years, there would have been no men’s footy on this weekend at all. Instead, 172,000 people went along and millions more watched on TV. This is actually a flimsier argument than it sounds. The AFL created the bye weekend a few years ago, and now it uses the wildcard as an answer to fixing the problem of having that bye. Groucho Marx might be consulting. The business case says the raw numbers, the money generated, the people attracted to watch the game make wildcard an overwhelming success. Clearly the biggest wildcard round they’ve ever had! Wildcard crowds Western Bulldogs vs Collingwood (Friday night): 81,036

Melbourne vs Carlton (Saturday night): 91,733 By comparison, the NRL this week had viewing numbers about half the AFL’s. Cute.

Advertisement

So the reasoning is the eyeballs are on the AFL and not drifting to other things, and those huge crowds engendered excitement when otherwise (for male football, there is still the AFLW) there would have been the high drama of … a legends’ match. But this year they had Collingwood one night and Carlton the next. Of course they got crowds and TV numbers like that. If next year’s wildcard round is North Melbourne v Gold Coast and GWS v Port Adelaide, and the numbers are barely a fraction of this year’s, will the AFL say “well that didn’t work, look at the crowds”? Blues fans could be forgiven for struggling to believe what they’re seeing. AFL Photos For the team that finishes 10th in a competition of 18 to be rewarded with a chance to play finals remains illogical.

Advertisement

Melbourne, who finished the regular season 10 points – two and a half wins – ahead of Carlton had to play a side that was rewarded for two thirds of a great season. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The Blues never dreamed of coming this far. The Cats are next in their sights The football on Friday night was tense and tight and a cracking game that finished after the siren. But it also had the feel of eighth playing ninth. The argument to counter the idea of a lack of integrity inherent in rewarding mediocre teams is that wildcard is another AFL retrofit to fix other fixturing problems. Maybe it is fair to give a chance to two sides that might have finished outside the old final eight only by virtue of the compromised fixture. Maybe that compromised fixture punished them more than the teams above them with short breaks, cross-country travel (clearly not Collingwood’s reason for finishing ninth), the number of terrible versus terrific teams they played … or coaches they had to sack mid-year.

Advertisement

Wildcard round will continue because it was high drama. The football was thrilling, tight throughout both games, intense, pressured and great theatre. One bloke hit the post four times, the best small forward in the game missed shots he would usually kick, the two best players in the competition went head-to-head and both played well. Carlton and Collingwood are box-office teams, so drama follows them. But when one plays in a game decided after the siren and the other is riding a wave and in-season turnaround unseen in football, then that drama captivates everyone. The wildcard round meant Carlton’s ride was not forced to end this year in Shakespearean (wispy half-back, good on his left, played at the Globe) drama, achingly short of finals. View post on X The greatest gift the wildcard gave was keeping alive the best storyline of the year. No one – save for Melbourne who, were enjoying an extraordinary turnaround under a new coach of their own (and OK probably also a lot of people who just hate Carlton) – wanted to see the Josh Fraser transformation stop here. Now the Blues play Geelong, a team they have beaten the past three times.

Advertisement

Carlton’s story has delivered the AFL the narrative to go with the economics. Friday night was a close, tough game where it felt like Bulldogs should be five goals clear for most of the night, but Craig McRae’s Collingwood have a gift for competing and staying in touch. It ended in a missed shot at goal after the siren. This actually shouldn’t have been a surprise, it was the fourth Collingwood game this year decided by a kick on or after the siren. Related Article AFL 2026 How the Blues are harnessing the energy of their boisterous fans to ‘break’ rivals Football likes to present itself as romantic (there is no other reason to have the father-son rule), but business pragmatism is always more compelling. Without getting into the weeds, romance delivered Tasmania a team, but business delivered Tasmania a roofed-stadium-or-bust ultimatum that was not demanded of either Gold Coast or GWS in the states the AFL’s marketeers coveted. Romance only goes so far. This wildcard round of quasi-finals, or round 25 if you’re Ed Richards, has given the AFL the most perfect weekend it could have hoped for. It doesn’t necessarily make it the right thing for football, but it makes it the concept that is here to say. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. title: Trump’s Venezuela oil deal has seismic potential, but it’s an idea not a reality
text:
Advertisement

Analysis WorldNorth AmericaOil Trump’s Venezuela oil deal has seismic potential, but it’s an idea not a reality Michael Koziol August 30, 2026 — 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: As far as announcements go, it was pretty low-key. Word came from US President Donald Trump’s Truth Social account just before 7pm on Friday, a time slot typically reserved for bad news you want to bury. Instead, Trump unveiled an unprecedented deal for the US to take control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, in what he billed as the largest such agreement in world history. Donald Trump has his sights set on unlocking Venezuela’s oil. Marija Ercegovac “This Historic Transaction MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves, greatly increases our Oil Supply, and will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future, while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity,” he said. There have been no documents to accompany the announcement, and few details – though Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, provided some information.

Advertisement

She said the deal called for the development of 17 strategic oil fields, with proven potential of 65 billion barrels. It would involve an investment of $US100 billion ($140 billion) and it would yield “more than $US209 billion” in tax revenue for Venezuela, she said. Related Article Trump diplomacy Trump says US has agreed to deal with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves With Trump, we are used to brash overselling of achievements and deals. But in this case, the upside for both nations has the capacity to be significant – if it ever comes to fruition. Venezuela is in a parlous state and it was so for many years under the dictatorial socialist regime of Nicolás Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell on trial for drug trafficking (he and his wife have pleaded not guilty). Its ability to harvest the world’s largest proven oil reserves, some 303 billion barrels, was badly compromised, though things have started to turn around since Maduro was captured by US forces and Rodriguez was installed.

Advertisement

The beneficiary has been the United States. At a time when it has had to draw down its Strategic Petroleum Reserves to compensate for the supply shock caused by the war in Iran, the US has dramatically increased oil imports from Venezuela. In December, before Maduro was captured, the US imported 4.26 million barrels of Venezuelan crude oil and petroleum products. By May, that figure had risen to 16.85 million. Venezuela is now the US’s second-largest overseas source of oil, behind only Canada. But to go beyond that will require significant investment from American oil companies, something they have thus far been reluctant to entertain. However, Chevron, the second-largest US oil firm and the only one with a sizeable presence in Venezuela, is in talks to expand its operations. Trump’s deal is aimed at beginning this process. A US official said it gave the US 55 per cent of the effective output from a new private joint venture, split between holding company equity and at-cost offtake for the federal government. The venture will become the second-largest private oil company in the world by reserves, after Saudi Aramco.

Advertisement

Nicolás Maduro was unceremoniously removed from power by the US in a bold military raid in January. NYT “As the company scales production, the resulting stable supply of at-cost oil in our hemisphere will go toward filling the US strategic petroleum reserve and fulfilling the supply needs of our great US military,” the official said. So, this is a long-term play, and it is certainly not one that will lower petrol prices for US motorists now. Enticing billions in investment from US companies also depends on continued stability in Venezuela. To that end, it remains unclear if and when elections will be held in that country. “They’re not really ready for them yet,” Trump said in July. Talks in Venezuela – which the US says it is facilitating, not dictating – are led by Jorge Rodriguez, the brother of Delcy Rodriguez and president of the National Assembly, and former politician Dinorah Figuera, a relatively obscure figure representing the opposition.

Advertisement

Related Article Venezuela crisis Stealth drones and massive blowtorches: How the US mission to capture Maduro unfolded Politico reported on Sunday that the talks were largely taking place at the JW Marriott hotel in central Caracas, which has acted as ground zero for US activity in the capital since Maduro’s removal. American energy company executives “broker deals in the lobby”, according to Politico. Trump made no secret from the outset that gaining access to Venezuela’s enormous oil reserves was a top factor, maybe the overriding one, in his decision to kidnap Maduro at the start of the year. He told reporters he had briefed oil company chiefs in advance and he said they couldn’t wait to go in and start taking the oil. In theory, sure – but in practice, it is still a huge risk. And how will this apparent deal be seen by Venezuelans? After all, it’s an agreement struck between the Trump administration and an interim president who serves with Washington’s imprimatur – not a deal made with any legitimately elected government.

Advertisement

Indeed, it underlines that Trump’s priority is to exploit Venezuela’s oil, not to bring democracy to Caracas. Venezuela has some of the world’s largest proven oil reserves, but unlocking its potential will take huge investment after years of decline. AP Rafael Ramirez, who was energy minister under former Venezuelan president Hugo Chavez, and president of the state-owned oil company PDVSA at the same time, said the deal was “another ambush” by the Americans. “It will go down in history for being a sellout and for opening the doors to the new colonialism of the United States,” he said on X. “An agreement behind the country’s back, clearly unconstitutional, that cedes control of the territory and the oil to a foreign power.” Emmanuel Rincón, a Miami-based political consultant focusing on Latin America, said Trump “has handed the anti-imperialist Latin American left a powerful weapon that they will use to win elections for decades”.

Two years ago, after Raul Carrera tore up his meniscus, doctors told him he would never run again. On Sunday, the Arizona native proved them wrong when he crossed the finish line at the Sydney Marathon.

Slumped over the barricade, tears streaming down his face, Carrera sobbed. “I am here. I did it.”

An emotional Raul Carrera after finishing the Sydney Marathon. Audrey Richardson

“There were times I really wanted to quit,” Carrera said. “I got to Mrs Macquarie’s Chair and thought I wasn’t going to make it, but I just kept putting one foot in front of the other.”

Under a clear azure sky, they came in their thousands, the atmosphere electric. One did not need to be a runner to be swept up in marathon mania. Spectators on the sideline whooped, cheered and whistled to energise the passing throng. Among the runners were famous faces including Olympian Emma McKeon, three-time Grand Slam singles winner Ash Barty and Olympian boxer Harry Garside.

McKeon, a six-time Olympic gold medallist and one of the best freestyle swimmers in Australian history, finished in a time of 4:41:30.

Six-time Olympic gold medal winner Emma McKeon after finishing the Sydney Marathon. Audrey Richardson

After Sydney gained World Marathon Major status, this year, 123,000 people entered the ballot, vying for just 40,000 spots. With no priority given to local runners, thousands missed out. Some showed up anyway.

“You got my ballot spot – enjoy it,” read one sign.

Jenny Tran, who missed out on an entry, ran along the sidelines to cheer on her friend. “It’s so empowering. Everyone is so positive,” she said, adding that she planned to try and sneak onto the track for the final two kilometres.

In the elite field, Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir was crowned the women’s champion, finishing in 02:18:31 to add Sydney to her major victories in Boston, New York and London.

Addisu Gobena wins the Sydney Marathon. Audrey Richardson

In the men’s division, 21-year-old Ethiopian Addisu Gobena – a javelin thrower until 2023 – shattered the course record by almost a minute and a half, crossing the line in 2:04:42.

At the 12km mark, in the shadow of the Cahill Expressway, runners were met with energy shots, blasting music and an emcee amping up the crowd.

“It’s wonderful. It is early, but it feels like the middle of the afternoon,” said spectator Christian Torres from Mexico. “My job is to cheer on my friend and other people. As a runner, it cheers you up a lot and gives you a boost.”

As runners exited the Sydney Harbour Bridge, one woman waved a homemade poster: “Welcome to Sydney. That’ll be $8.50.” Another crowd-pleasing sign spotted in the crowd: “Pain is temporary but Strava is forever.”

Thousands of runners cross the Sydney Harbour Bridge for the marathon. George Chan

For spectators like Nicolas Soares, simply watching the runners was enough to get his heart pumping. “Everything is beautiful. It’s a perfect day for running. Not too hot, not too cold. It’s beautiful”, he said.

The marathon split the city like a river. With roads closed for the steady stream of athletes, pedestrians lined up to be ushered across the track. For a few seconds, they too were part of the marathon.

At the Opera House finish line, best friends Charlotte Forelich and Shannon McIvor wept after completing their first – and last – marathon, propelled through Sydney’s famously punishing hills by what McIvor called “radical delusion”.

“I am in pain,” Forelich said. “It was amazing, but it was mentally very challenging. I think I stopped at 30 kilometres for a little cry, but I’m still here.”

Rosslyne and Michael Wilson have a moment at the finish line. George Chan

Emotions were high for spectators. Rosslyne Wilson, mother of runner Michael Wilson, had tears streaming down her face as her son crossed the finish line.

“He has done an amazing job. He is so hard on himself. He is so brilliant,” she said.

The proud mother told the Herald her son had recently run 100 kilometres around a Bendigo athletics track to raise money for bowel cancer.

Amid the lycra was the occasional costume. Phil Brent, dressed head to toe as a turtle, broke a Guinness World Record for “fastest marathon dressed in a reptile costume”. He had just a single training run in the outfit. “I ran around my local area at nighttime. I didn’t want anyone to see me,” Brent said.

Phil Brent poses with his Sydney Marathon medal and his new world record. Audrey Richardson

Perched on her partner’s shoulders, Central Coast woman Tayla Mackay was on top of the world.

It was the 25-year-old’s second marathon, and she smashed her personal best. Despite being “very sore and very tired”, Mackay was buzzing. “I cried when I saw my mum. I think I’m going to have to do all the world majors now.”

But for now, Mackay was off to a much-awaited destination: the pub.

The Wallabies continued their winning ways under new coach Les Kiss, posting their fourth straight win for the first time since 2021. Here’s our rating for each Wallabies player. 1. Isaac Kailea 5.5/10 In his first Test in 630 days, the mobile NSW prop looked to use his feet at the line with early carries. But was one of many to find it hard going against the Pumas’ defence and otherwise had limited involvements in his 40 minutes. Set-piece work was solid. Loading 2. Brandon Paenga-Amosa 7.5

Advertisement

BPA is a good example of how front-rowers age like a good red wine. A Malbec, perhaps. At the age of 30 and with a stint in France under his belt, the former garbo is now in the form of his life on all fronts: lineout throwing, scrummaging, defence, ball carrying and he’s also a consistent try sneak. Effort to be in the left corner to score in Jujuy deserves a toast. 3. Allan Alaalatoa 7 There is a good argument that an eyes-up back such as Ryan Lonergan should be looked as Wallabies captain when Harry Wilson doesn’t play. But then you see Alaalatoa lead like he did against the Pumas, and you understand why he gets the armband. Has a rare combination of calm and menace, and hits like a train. 4. Josh Canham 7.5 Quick reminder this guy was only playing in his seventh Test in Jujuy. It’s easy to overlook, given how much impact Canham brings as an athletic carrier, lineout operator and as one of the most effective ball handlers, as well. Always seems to have an offload ready.

Advertisement

5. Jeremy Williams 7.5 Returned to the starting line-up and turned in another high-quality 80-minute performance. At 113kg, Williams is on the lighter end of the scale for tighthead locks in Test rugby, but the Wallabies’ scrum doesn’t seem to suffer. His mobility and skill pay dividends in open play: see try assist for BPA. Tom Hooper of the Wallabies scores a try. Getty Images 6. Tom Hooper 8 Was always a workhorse but Hooper has become more of an athlete since joining Exeter, and that was shown with an 80-minute effort featuring 14 runs, 11 tackles, two key turnovers and the try that ultimately secured the game. Coming off a long break with a shoulder injury, it was very impressive and combined with the other two below, it makes picking a back row difficult for Les Kiss next week.

Advertisement

7. Fraser McReight 8 McReight has already had a superb year and the headgeared flanker now routinely gets ranked in the world’s top five back-rowers. And fair enough. Yet another all-singing, all-dancing display: one try, 11 carries, team-high 14 tackles and a late steal that denied Argentina a potential win. 8. Rob Valetini 8.5 Rob Valetini gets the ball away in traffic. Getty Images Are we totally sure big Bobby V isn’t part-machine? Back in the starting side after a rest in Townsville, and Valetini turned yet another powerhouse performance: team-high 17 carries and equal team-high tackles (14) with McReight, and a goal line turnover (we’ll forget the kick). Back at his favoured No.8 spot and such a luxury to have a guy who’ll quietly roll his sleeves up every single time he plays.

Advertisement

9. Ryan Lonergan 6.5 Solid effort in the first half, albeit with some missed tackles and a rare shank off the kicking tee. Left the field early in the second half after a head knock when making a try-saving cover tackle, but it was also due to a flu. 10. Carter Gordon 6.5 Nice to see Gordon getting through games and threatening the line with his under-rated running game and his sharp passing. Scored a good try with a hard line. Gordon’s kicking game is a strength, but we haven’t seen it in full flight yet. Short kicking might have been effective against the Pumas’ line speed, too. Carter Gordon of the Wallabies is challenged by Ignacio Mendy and Santiago Carreras. Getty Images

Advertisement

11. Harry Potter 5 A day of limited involvement for Potter on the left wing, with only a handful of runs and mixed results in the aerial contest space. Points off for spending 10 minutes in the sin bin after going for an unwise, low-percentage intercept with one hand. 12. Hunter Paisami 6.5 Plenty of tough carries, including the support run that saw Paisami break through and led to Hooper’s crucial try. Ikitau is every chance to return next week, but this has been an important block for Paisami to prove himself indispensable to Les Kiss’s squad going forward, even after he moves to Japan next year. 13. Isaac Henry 5.5

Advertisement

A quiet day was always going to come for Henry after the high-octane opening two Tests. The ball simply didn’t come his way much, in attack or defence. But nor did he make any major mistakes. Max Jorgensen celebrates after Australia’s win over Argentina. Getty Images 14. Max Jorgensen 7.5 Jorgensen made his name by being an open-field whiz, with incredible feet and deception. But Test rugby doesn’t give you as much space, so the youngster is now providing value in other ways: he is the Wallabies’ best man in the air, he is strong carrying in traffic and he can also muscle up in defence, as seen in Jujuy. 15. Tom Wright 5.5

Advertisement

Another who was solid but not spectacular, with mixed kicking outcomes and some wayward passing. Wright at his best is always threatening around the ball, particularly for the Brumbies, and it’d be good to see him lurking in closer channels for the Wallabies. Reserves 16. Billy Pollard 6.5 Always brings energy and fast leg-speed from the bench, but his massive hit in the last 10 minutes – that preceded McReight’s steal – showed the ex-leaguie still lurking in Pollard. Angus Bell 6.5

Advertisement

17. Solid 40-minue effort from Bell, but didn’t get the ball enough to see any of his trademark wind-up carrying. The Wallabies hung on to beat Argentina to make it four straight wins for the first time since 2021., Getty Images 18. Massimo De Lutiis 6.5 The Reds love big “Mass” for his power in contact, and we saw some of that with plenty of carries and some post-gainline metres, to boot. So far, showing he can handle Test rugby.

Advertisement

19. Lachlan Shaw 5.5 Has a bit of Canham about him in the athleticism, but Shaw is also learning on the job at Test level; he’d take back a loose flick pass in the second half that scuttled one attacking move. 20. Charlie Cale 6 Limited minutes from the bench, but grabbed a couple of pressure lineout wins in the dying stages that helped get Australia home. 21. Tate McDermott 6

Steady performance from the reserve halfback when he replaced Lonergan, but box kicking game is still not his forte, and the only glimpse of McDermott’s lethal running game led to a held-up. 22. Ben Donaldson 5 Almost 20 minutes on the field as a replacement for Gordon and Wright, but a missed conversion for Hooper’s try kept the game tight, and pushing a pass in the dying moments from a line break – that led to a turnover – was also unnecessary. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii throws a no-look pass. Getty Images 23. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii 7 Clearly was out to make an impact with his 15 minutes on the field, and the highly paid recruit did that with four carries and the second-most metres run in the whole team. title: 'Massive changes': What you might find missing in Aussie supermarkets
text:
In Brief A social media trend known as "sardinemaxxing" has seen sardines cleared from supermarket shelves after hot demand.

Experts say the social media trend could be dangerous for other fish.

Walk down the canned fish aisle at your local supermarket right now, and there's a good chance you'll find a gap where the tinned sardines used to be, as a viral TikTok trend sends a wave of new fans in search of the small, oily fish.

The trend, dubbed "sardinemaxxing", has seen influencers push sardines as a beauty and wellness must-have, with some calling them "Botox on a fork" for their purported skin, hair, and anti-ageing benefits.

But experts say the trend raises real questions about where those sardines are coming from — and what happens if the hype spreads to other seafood.

Why groceries are going viral

Sardines are just the latest grocery item swept up in a social media-driven buying frenzy.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Cottage cheese and Greek yoghurt both had their moment in the past year, part of a broader "proteinmaxxing" wave prizing high-protein foods.

Lisa Asher, a retail and supermarket expert at the University of Sydney Business School, said the pattern is driven by a mix of influencer culture and wellness trends.

"What bothers me isn't that the kids are eating sardines … it's that they're taking advice now from people who are probably not people you should be listening to," Asher said.

"It's a new form of advertising with a lot of unknowns — we don't really know who's paying who and how much they're making out of it. That is a problem.

"In magazines, we used to look at celebrities, but celebrities have been replaced by influencers."

She said the trends all follow a similar pattern: demand increases, the product goes out of stock, prices sometimes rise, and eventually, when the hype cools down, it comes back in stock.

"But this is a product that is made from fish in the sea," she adds. "We don't want to overfish because suddenly, then we have none."

Canned sardines can be hard to come by these days thanks to a new social media trend. Source: Getty / Newscast / Universal Images Group

The big catch

That's where the environmental risks come in.

Adrian Meder, sustainable seafood program manager at the Australian Marine Conservation Society, says history shows a sudden cultural appetite for a particular seafood can do serious damage — pointing to shark fin soup, sea cucumber and some tuna fisheries as species pushed towards collapse by surging demand.

"We've yet to see online popularity as a driver of major declines in our oceans, but a cultural surge in popularity of a seafood has time and time again decimated populations of species from tunas, to sharks, to abalone, to sea cucumbers," Meder told SBS News.

"Online popularity is clearly capable of producing massive changes in consumer demand."

There's also a traceability problem: much of the tinned sardines on Australian shelves is imported, and it can be difficult to know where a can came from or how sustainably it was caught.

Jonathan Smart, an affiliate senior research scientist at James Cook University, agrees that origin matters.

He co-authored a study, released last week, that found Australia ranked just 52nd in seafood production, despite having about eight million square kilometres of fishing waters.

"The fisheries that a lot of our imported seafood comes from are actually quite unsustainable — and Australia imports a lot of seafood when perhaps it shouldn't," Smart told SBS News.

"By importing so much seafood, we're essentially exporting our environmental footprint to other countries that don't have the same level of management that we do."

He worries a viral trend like this one could make that problem worse.

"If a trend like this is popping up and all of a sudden you've got greater consumption of a species, the fear I would have is that then is going to lead to, again, a greater surge in that imported seafood.

"We just don't know if that's going to have the same sustainability levels as if you were actually consuming something locally."

A resilient little fish

But of all the species to go viral, sardines might be one of the best placed to handle their 15 minutes of fame.

Smart says sardines are a fast-growing, short-lived species with rapid turnover, making them naturally resilient to heavy fishing.

Because changes in biomass are driven more by environmental conditions — like ocean upwellings — rather than fishing activity, sardine and anchovy fisheries are some of the biggest in the world, he said.

"They can actually provide a really, really big harvest from them normally under sustainable conditions, depending on the fishery that they're coming from."

Locally, there's also a genuine opportunity: Australia's biggest fishery is a sardine fishery in South Australia — a fact Smart says is little known because much of the catch goes to aquaculture feed.

"Very little of it actually goes to human consumption," he said. "That's why I often recommend to people that we should be eating more sardines because that is a really sustainable fishery.

"We catch a lot of fish from it, and there's a lot of opportunity."

Meder agrees that there's room for Australians to put more sardines on their plate.

"Some cultures, including many Australian communities, actually used to eat a lot more sardines than they do now," he said, pointing to a shift in seafood consumption to more environmentally vulnerable, less abundant, and expensive fish species — of which trends like these could help reverse.

But that only holds if the sardines on the shelf are actually Australian — which means consumers may need to check labels and do a bit of Googling before putting them in their shopping basket.

So while sardines may be getting the limelight for just a brief period before scrollers move on to the next trend, if there's anything we can take from it, it's that the humble little sardine is actually built for this moment.

title: What we know as Australia's bird flu outbreak enters a grim new chapter
text:
In brief A seal, a dolphin and a fox have tested positive for H5 bird flu in South Australia.

Experts share advice on protecting pets and wildlife as the outbreak grows.

Bird flu has begun its spread beyond birds in Australia, with cases confirmed in three different mammal species since last weekend.

On Friday, Australia's chief veterinary officer, Beth Cookson, said H5 bird flu had been confirmed in a red fox found in metropolitan Adelaide, marking the first in a land mammal in Australia.

A dead dolphin found on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula also tested positive this week, days after a long-nosed fur seal found dead at Beachport became the country's first mainland mammal case.

How does bird flu spread in mammals?

Bird flu has been detected in many different mammals on other continents, including cats and dogs, farm animals, dolphins, seals, foxes, tigers, leopards and polar bears.
