Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Infected birds spread the virus through droppings, feathers and other bodily fluids. It can also be transmitted via contaminated clothing, footwear, equipment and vehicles.

Under favourable conditions, the virus can survive in the environment for months, Australian government authorities have said.

While the virus primarily spreads from infected birds, there is evidence it can also spread between some mammals, including during outbreaks in seals and dairy cattle overseas.

READ MORE 'Contaminated': How deadly bird flu crossed a new threshold in Australia

Among scavengers like foxes and cats, infections have been linked to eating or interacting with bird carcasses.

Cookson said there was no evidence of mammal-to-mammal transmission of the virus in Australia.

"This detection in a fox is a good reminder that people and their pets should avoid sick or dead wildlife," Cookson said on Friday.

READ MORE Rush to vaccinate little penguins against H5N1 as another seal is diagnosed

"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected given that H5 bird flu has been detected in other wildlife in areas where there are high levels of infection in wild birds."

She said the risk to human health remains low.

Which Australian mammals are most at risk?

The government's H5 bird flu risk assessment ranks multiple dolphin, seal and sea lion species among Australia's most vulnerable native mammals, and experts fear the virus could have devastating consequences for endangered species such as the Australian sea lion.

Seal populations around the world have proved particularly vulnerable to bird flu outbreaks.

The virus decimated southern elephant seal populations on Heard Island after reaching the Australian sub-antarctic territory last year, killing an estimated 75 per cent of pups.

Jane Younger, senior lecturer in Southern Ocean vertebrate ecology at the University of Tasmania, said it was "devastating news for wildlife" that bird flu had been detected in a mainland Australian mammal.

"My biggest concern now is the endangered Australian sea lion, which is found nowhere else in the world," she said.

"Infected and dying seabirds have already been found at important sea lion breeding sites around Kangaroo Island. If the virus enters a breeding colony, there is no way to stop it spreading."

She called for intensive surveillance of seal and sea lion colonies, rapid genome sequencing of mammal cases and an urgent investigation of whether targeted vaccinations could help protect certain populations.

South Australian Environment Minister Emily Bourke said last week that her state would assess the possibility of importing an experimental US vaccine for use among mammals in Australia, but warned that vaccines for mammals such as cattle and cats being developed overseas are yet to be approved by authorities.

The use of vaccines in birds is further advanced, with Australian officials saying last year that a H5 vaccine had been procured and authorised for use in particular rare, protected or valuable bird populations.

Victoria is currently vaccinating thousands of little penguins, which are a popular tourist attraction.

Should we be worried about our cats and dogs?

Bird flu infections have been reported in domestic cats and dogs overseas, though the Australian government says such infections are uncommon and usually occur through contact with infected birds.

Symptoms may include fever, lethargy, decreased appetite, red or inflamed eyes, discharge from eyes and nose, coughing and sneezing, and tremors.

Cat owners should be particularly mindful, Robyn Alders, an animal influenza expert and honorary professor at the Australian National University's Crawford School of Public Health, told SBS News.

Overseas, cats infected with the virus have experienced a high mortality rate.

She suggests keeping cats indoors, especially in areas where bird flu cases have been confirmed, and keeping dogs on a leash when walking.

The virus can also be spread through contaminated food and water, so experts recommend keeping pets' bowls inside or out of reach of wild birds.

Australians visiting wetlands, beaches, farms or wildlife areas are advised to observe wildlife from a distance, avoid contact with sick or dead animals, and to clean footwear and equipment with detergent or disinfectant.

Alders suggests that pet owners who go for walks in areas where sick or dead animals have been found could consider keeping a separate pair of walking shoes that they always disinfect.

title: More Australians are buying homes later. What does that mean for retirement?
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Damian Hole's last mortgage repayment is due when he's 80.

The 52-year-old bought his first home about a decade ago and refinanced it in 2024, locking in a new 30-year loan term just before he turned 50.

He's among a growing cohort of Australians buying their first home later in life. People over the age of 40 accounted for nearly one in five first-home buyers last year (18.7 per cent), according to data from one of Australia's largest mortgage brokers, Aussie Home Loans.

That's up from just over 5.5 per cent in 2005.

At the other end, people under the age of 20 made up around a quarter of first-home buyers in 2005, compared with less than 0.5 per cent in 2025.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

As housing affordability pressures make it harder for young Australians to enter the market, solutions designed to ease the path to home ownership have increasingly focused on expanding access to credit — allowing buyers to borrow more, with smaller deposits or longer mortgage terms.

Low-deposit loans can be accessed through the federal government's 5 per cent deposit scheme, while family guarantor loans allow first-time buyers to borrow up to 100 per cent of the purchase price.

A growing cohort of Australians are buying their first home later in life. Source: SBS News

Meanwhile, more lenders are offering 40-year mortgage terms, meaning some borrowers could be signing up to make repayments well into their later years.

If a growing number of Australians are buying homes later while taking on larger loans for longer, what happens when they reach retirement still saddled with mortgage debt?

'A cat and mouse game'

Making it easier for people to borrow can fuel higher house prices.

According to James Graham, a housing economics expert at the University of Sydney, without massively expanding housing supply, broadening access to credit alone is not a sustainable solution.

"It's just sort of a cat-and-mouse game," Graham tells SBS News.

"The prices go up, so we change mortgage credit. That pushes prices up further.

People are just borrowing more to buy more expensive houses, and they're not really any better off.

When the government introduced its 5 per cent deposit scheme last year, designed to help first-home buyers, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) predicted the measure would likely "put at least some further upward pressure" on housing price growth.

By March, the value of new loans taken out by first-home buyers was around 11 per cent higher than before the scheme was expanded in October, with the increase largely reflecting bigger average loan sizes, according to the RBA.

The costs of delayed home ownership

Graham says buying a first home later in life could have consequences beyond carrying mortgage debt into retirement. Entering the market at 40 or 50 leaves less time to build housing wealth and can reduce people's ability to move as their lives change.

"People are likely to be locked in for longer," he explains, warning that some buyers may end up remaining in homes that were intended as a first step into the market rather than a last stop.

"Less moving has its own social consequences," he adds.

"It means that people can't move back to communities that they wanted to be part of; they're further away from their children than they wanted to be; they're not near jobs that they want to be near.

"Maybe they've moved far out of the city because that's the only place they could buy. But now they're away from amenities and doctors."

Delayed home ownership and larger mortgages could also have implications for the aged care sector. Traditionally, many older Australians have relied on accessing housing equity (the portion of a property that is owned outright) to help fund retirement living or aged care, often through selling the family home. Unsettled mortgage debt could affect this transition, reducing the overall equity available.

Another concern is long-term mortgage stress, which can reduce the wellbeing of older Australians and may lead retirees to draw down their superannuation to pay off housing debt, according to 2019 research from the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI).

This, in turn, could place additional pressure on the pension system.

Currently, the Age Pension excludes the primary home from its assets test.

Paying down mortgage debt on a primary home with super can, therefore, reduce a person's assessable assets and potentially make them eligible for the pension.

"We have an ageing population in Australia, so the fiscal pressure on government will increase with that if government is supporting people through the pension system," AHURI managing director Tom Alves tells SBS News.

"The compulsory superannuation system is designed to address that issue, and if people are not having enough income through their super because they've used it to pay off their mortgage, obviously that's an issue."

AHURI's research notes that mortgage debt was uncommon among people aged 55-64 as early as the 1990s. Between 1996 and 2013, however, the proportion of Australians in that age bracket still paying off a mortgage rose from under 20 per cent to 45 per cent.

Home ownership has long underpinned Australia's retirement system, with policies, including the Age Pension, built on the assumption that most retirees own their home.

Widely used superannuation savings targets typically assume that people will own their homes outright by the time they reach retirement. While some modelling also considers renters, retirees still paying off a mortgage are largely left out of the picture.

"They do assume that people own their home," Susan Thorp, a retirement finance specialist at Monash University, tells SBS News.

"They're not allowing for the idea that someone may have, say, $150,000 of mortgage debt at the time they're retiring."

Yet a growing share of Australians may not fit those assumptions. In a January survey of 1,020 people by Loan Market Group, 58 per cent said they planned to own their home before retirement.

The rise of the 40-year mortgage

A small but growing number of Australian lenders have started offering 40-year mortgage terms, which can give borrowers access to loans they might not otherwise have been able to afford — but can add staggering extra interest costs over the life of the loan.

Source: SBS News

Richard Brown, a Mortgage Choice broker in the Sydney suburb of Epping, says many of his clients are eager to find ways to maximise their borrowing power, which is increasing their appetite for longer loan terms despite the downsides.

"There's an appetite for borrowers to get access to the money they need to buy the property they want," he says.

"They don't care what it is."

Sebastian Watkins, CEO and co-founder of mortgage broking giant Lendi Group, says relying on borrowing innovations like longer loan terms risks overlooking the underlying issue of unaffordable housing prices.

"We can't simply respond to people taking longer to save by giving them longer to pay off their loan," he tells SBS News.

If current trends continue, in a decade or two, Watkins expects the average Australian mortgage to be "larger, held later in life and managed much more dynamically".

We are likely to see longer loan terms, more family-supported or multi-generational borrowing and products that adapt as a customer's income, family circumstances and property needs change.

Japan offers an extreme historical example of intergenerational borrowing. Amid soaring housing costs in the 1980s, it experimented with 100-year mortgages designed to be repaid across multiple generations. Researchers who later modelled the loans concluded they did little to improve housing affordability.

What happens when debt stretches beyond careers?

Lenders assessing older applicants will typically look for a credible exit strategy demonstrating the loan can be comfortably managed in retirement, Watkins says.

"They may look at the expected loan balance at retirement age and consider the borrower's projected superannuation and other assets. Another potential strategy could be downsizing, where the borrower could sell the property and purchase a lower-value home," he says.

Hole, who bought his first home at 42, says his bank requested his superannuation balance before approving his mortgage.

"It was almost done, and then they requested my super balance, and then I realised, because my age will go beyond retirement, they're just seeing if I've got enough super to pay off the loan."

He says he should be able to comfortably repay the remainder of his mortgage with a lump sum from his super when he reaches retirement age, at which point he intends to access the Age Pension.

Damian Hole, 52, lives in Bacchus Marsh, Victoria, with his wife and three kids. Source: Supplied

The retirement debt challenge

Alves says there is no single policy fix, but governments need to consider both retirement and housing policy together.

Potential approaches include adjusting Age Pension settings to better reflect the differences between homeowners and non-homeowners, as well as expanding affordable housing options for older Australians, he says.

More broadly, he says improving access to home ownership earlier in life and increasing the supply of affordable rental housing could help reduce the number of Australians entering retirement with housing stress.

Thorp says there are fundamental questions that remain unanswered about what happens when more Australians enter retirement with housing debt.

"The question of how housing policy merges with superannuation and retirement policy is not fully worked out," she says.

title: Australian woman feared missing in Nepal flood makes contact as disaster worsens
text:
Australian authorities are urgently trying to reach a woman who made contact with family after surviving catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-China border.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) is engaging with local authorities on plans to assist the woman, who is understood to have been last reported in a remote area several days' hike from Kathmandu.

At least 38 Australians remain missing after an ice avalanche on Wednesday triggered Nepal's worst natural disaster in more than a decade.

Heavy continued rainfall is making rescue conditions difficult and unpredictable.

Further severe flooding, landslides and debris flows are predicted in the affected areas of Nepal and Tibet while a lake formed by the landslide has started to overflow.

At least 538 people have died, Nepalese authorities said, while almost 1,000 remain missing.

Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was on a pilgrimage on the China-Nepal border when the catastrophic flash flooding hit.

Her husband Kailash Mansowar, who has not heard from her since, has travelled to the region from Sydney to find her, guided only by her iPhone's last location.

"I am here in Nepal now (since) yesterday and working with local authorities to find further information," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) on Friday.

Like many missing Australians, Adhikari was undertaking a group tour, in her case with the Isha Foundation.

She left Kathmandu on 14 August after flying from Sydney to trek to a sacred site near Tibet's Mount Kailash.

"Even the smallest piece of information could help bring her home," a widely shared post on social media announcing her disappearance reads.

A separate group of 15 Australians, including two boys aged 11 and 14, were travelling with US-based tourism operator Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company.

Sydney doctor Manoj Dharmaratnam, who was invited to join the sacred pilgrimage but chose not to go, prescribed several of his friends altitude medication and conducted injury assessments before they left Australia.

"One of them had an injury and I did tell her, maybe you're not fit to go on this trek," Dr Dharmaratnam told AAP.

"She actually called up and cancelled her trip ... but then she said I've bought the ticket, so I might as well go."

The Himalayan Glacier group included a well-respected Sydney couple with two sons in their 20s, both studying medicine in NSW, he said.

READ MORE How Australians can help those impacted by devastating Nepal floods

At least four Australians were travelling separately to tour groups, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Friday.

Wong said the federal government would send additional personnel to the region and unveiled a $5 million assistance package and humanitarian support.

An initial team of three humanitarian response specialists will be sent to help 20 staff already on the ground in Nepal.

But Chinese and Nepalese authorities say local rescue efforts could be complicated by further flooding, caused by a build-up of debris.

READ MORE Nepal's glacier collapse sends a warning beyond the Himalayas

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Thursday warned a lake was forming above the Rasuwagadhi border.

By Friday it had begun to overflow.

The Lhendi River had been obstructed about 18 kilometres above the border, posing a risk to residents in areas below, it said in a statement on social media.

The threat of a second flood caused by a blockage upstream led to evacuation orders at Jilong Port on the Nepal-China border, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

Rocks, boulders and debris lodged in the valley, as well as lakes forming along the plateau, could cause further flooding, geoscientist Jakob Steiner told AAP.

"Unfortunately it's not over ... this material is only going to lie there. We cannot move it away," Steiner, a fellow at the Asian Mountain Alliance, said.

"Every time a new flood comes, it's going to move this, and this is just going to increase future flood events in terms of impact."

title: How Australians can help those impacted by devastating Nepal floods
text:
IN BRIEF Donations will help provide emergency shelter, food, clean water, hygiene supplies and medical care.

Australians can donate through the Emergency Action Alliance's Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal or by calling 1300 939 000.

Entire communities have been devastated by severe flooding and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border, with homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure destroyed.

Search and rescue operations remain underway, while thousands of people are in urgent need of shelter, food, clean drinking water and medical assistance.

In response, 14 Australian charities have joined forces to launch a national appeal.

Emergency Action Alliance

The Emergency Action Alliance (EAA) has launched the Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal, bringing together a variety of charities to support communities affected by the disaster.

Australians are encouraged to donate through the EAA website or by calling 1300 939 000.

The charities participating in the appeal are Save the Children Australia, Plan International Australia, Oxfam Australia, Australia for UNHCR, ActionAid Australia, CARE Australia, Caritas Australia, ADRA, Act for Peace, Anglican Overseas Aid, Australian Lutheran World Service, Baptist World Aid Australia, CBM Australia and Tearfund Australia.

EAA executive director Kerren Morris said the appeal provided Australians with a trusted way to support people affected by the disaster.

"Emergency shelter, food, safe drinking water and medical support are urgently needed now, while longer-term recovery efforts will continue for many months," she said in a statement.

What are the charities doing?

The charities involved bring different areas of humanitarian expertise to the response, with organisations and their local partners working to provide immediate assistance to affected communities.

Save the Children Australia

Save the Children is focusing on supporting children and families affected by humanitarian emergencies.

Oxfam Australia

Oxfam Australia's humanitarian work includes support for essential services such as clean water, sanitation and emergency assistance.

Australia for UNHCR

Australia for UNHCR is the UN refugee agency's national partner in Australia, and is supporting humanitarian assistance through the UNHCR network.

Homes and buildings have been left damaged and filled with debris after devastating flash floods swept through communities in Nepal. Source: Getty / Anadolu / Sunil Pradhan

What happens to donations?

The charities involved are continuing to assess the scale of the disaster and humanitarian needs in affected communities.

The EAA says its members are working to determine where support is most urgently needed as search and rescue operations continue.

The appeal has been endorsed by the Australian Council for International Development (ACFID), the peak body for Australian non-government organisations involved in humanitarian action and international development.

The ABC is also supporting the appeal through its ABC Gives initiative.

ACFID CEO Matthew Maury said coordinated action was critical as humanitarian needs continued to emerge.

"This appeal provides Australians with a trusted and effective way to support communities affected by this disaster," he said.

Australia pledges $5 million in aid

The Australian government has confirmed a $5 million humanitarian assistance package for communities affected by the devastating floods along the Nepal-China border.

The funding will support both the immediate disaster response and longer-term recovery, with the government saying it will help provide food, emergency shelter, clean water and sanitation.

READ MORE Nepal's glacier collapse sends a warning beyond the Himalayas

The $5 million package will be delivered through established humanitarian partners, including $2 million to the World Food Programme for food and logistical support, $2 million through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership for emergency assistance including shelter, hygiene kits, blankets, medical care and psychosocial support, and $1 million to the EAA to support locally led recovery and rehabilitation efforts.

Assistant Foreign Affairs Minister Matt Thistlethwaite said Australian officials were working with Nepali authorities and tour operators to understand the situation and assess the needs of those affected.

Thistlethwaite also said the government was "working around the clock" to verify the status of Australians in the region, but damaged roads and telecommunications infrastructure were making it difficult to establish contact.

More Australian support on the way

Australia will also deploy three humanitarian specialists to Nepal within 48 hours to help assess needs and support the emergency response.

The specialists are being deployed through the Australia Assists program and have expertise in humanitarian assessment, logistics, communications and planning.

A crisis response team member and a regional consular officer are already on the ground in Kathmandu, alongside staff at the Australian embassy.

Australians in the affected region

Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the scale of the disaster and the remoteness of the affected region meant there were "immense challenges" ahead for the response and recovery.

"With roads and bridges destroyed, many communities remain isolated and difficult to reach, underscoring the need for rapid humanitarian assistance," she said.

The government's humanitarian response comes as Australian officials continue to try to establish the whereabouts of Australians caught up in the disaster.

The latest government figure is at least 39 Australians reported missing.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is working with Nepali authorities, tour operators and others to verify their welfare and contact their families.

Australians requiring emergency consular assistance can contact the 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135 in Australia or +61 2 6261 3305 from overseas.

The government is also urging Australians in affected areas to follow the advice of local authorities and monitor official travel advice.

title: Questions were mounting at the border. Then they found a tunnel
text:
In brief A migrant tunnel between Belarus and Latvia has deepened a longstanding rift.

The tunnel's discovery has widened an already deep rift between the two countries.

Latvia's border guard has accused Belarusian authorities of partial responsibility for a recently discovered migrant tunnel beneath a border fence between the two nations.

The tunnel was uncovered by Latvian authorities in early August. Latvia faces an increasing number of migrants trying to cross the border from Belarus, further straining relations between the two countries.

Latvia shares a 173km border with Belarus. Latvia is a member of the European Union. Belarus, an independent nation with an authoritarian government, is not.

At the time of the tunnel's discovery, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said criminal networks were facilitating migration from Belarus into Latvia, bringing migrants into Europe's borderless Schengen area, but that the migrants' final destination was elsewhere on the continent.

"They migrate to where it's easier (to enter the EU). So we must not be the easiest place," Kulbergs told the press conference.

He pledged to target networks transporting the migrants from the border to their destinations, as well as any support points for migrants in Latvia, as part of what he called "Operation Werewolf".

"If everything goes according to plan, we are confident that we will already deal a serious enough blow to the system," Kulbergs said. "I want to tell the organisers: everything will be put to an end."

Latvia's government said in a statement it would cooperate with neighbours Estonia, Lithuania, Poland and others to stop the flow of migrants.

Latvia, along with Lithuania and Poland, has frequently accused Belarus' authoritarian government of smuggling migrants from crisis-impacted regions close to the EU's far borders.

The plot thickens

Having now discovered a second tunnel at another point along the border fence, Latvia is pointing fingers at the Belarusian border guard.

"It is simply impossible to build such a tunnel without the Belarusian border guards being aware of it," Guntis Pujats, head of the agency, told Latvian radio on Thursday.

Pujats went on to give more information about the original tunnel, saying that the entrance on the Belarusian side of the border was found around 10m from the border line and had been hidden among trees and bushes. The tunnel itself was reported to be 80cm wide and to run for roughly 30m.

Some 28 cubic metres of earth had been removed to construct the tunnel. Support structures had been erected within the tunnel to keep it from collapsing, and a plywood cover had been fitted to the entrance.

"The construction work was quite extensive. So the relevant authorities were undoubtedly aware of it," he said.

Pujats claimed that 12 underground tunnels have been found across Lithuania, along with the two found in Latvia to date.

The Belarusian government has not publicly commented on the existence of the tunnels.

title: France's cheese makers are confronting a problem tradition alone can't solve
text:
In brief A summer of record-breaking heatwaves and drought has taken a toll on France.

The unusually hot and dry conditions have started to affect France's beloved and protected cheesemakers.

Widespread drought and record-breaking heatwaves have forced France to relax some of its famously strict rules on cheese production, with authorities announcing special measures for abondance, beaufort and comte.

France's vast array of local cheeses are a source of national pride, and authorities go to great lengths to protect traditional production methods and ensure authenticity.

To earn a coveted "appellation d'origine protegee" (Protected Designation of Origin) label — and the right to give their cheese a particular protected name — producers must follow rigid rules on where their animals graze and what they eat.

But the summer's drought, which affected 95 per cent of mainland France in July, has left normally rich pastures dry and bare.

In response, the government said this week that producers of abondance, beaufort and comte, hard cheeses made from the raw milk of cows grazing in the Alps and Jura mountains, can supplement the animals' diet with more fodder and grain brought in from elsewhere.

Growth on permanent grasslands as of 10 August is a third less than the 1989-2018 average, according to the agriculture ministry's statistical service.

The fodder situation is "highly degraded" in almost all regions, the ministry said earlier this month.

The National Institute of Origin and Quality (INAO), the government agency that administers and enforces rules of origin, says it will also grant temporary relief for several other cheeses including reblochon, cantal, bleu d'Auvergne, and fourme d'Ambert.

Europe's record-breaking summer heat has caused thousands of excess deaths, set wildfires blazing and seen major rivers drop to record lows.

In France, farmers are bracing for their smallest corn crop since 1980, and winegrowers are reporting some of the earliest harvests on record.

Scientists say human-caused climate change has intensified the drought, with extreme heat rather than low rainfall driving the dry conditions.

title: Nepal army races to save 100 people trapped in tunnel as flood death toll rises over 530
text:

Nepali army helicopter rescue teams were working on Friday to rescue around 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by a devastating flood two days earlier.

In recent years, there would have been no men’s footy on this weekend at all. Instead, 172,000 people went along and millions more watched on TV. This is actually a flimsier argument than it sounds. The AFL created the bye weekend a few years ago, and now it uses the wildcard as an answer to fixing the problem of having that bye. Groucho Marx might be consulting. The business case says the raw numbers, the money generated, the people attracted to watch the game make wildcard an overwhelming success. Clearly the biggest wildcard round they’ve ever had! Wildcard crowds Western Bulldogs vs Collingwood (Friday night): 81,036

Melbourne vs Carlton (Saturday night): 91,733 By comparison, the NRL this week had viewing numbers about half the AFL’s. Cute.

Advertisement

So the reasoning is the eyeballs are on the AFL and not drifting to other things, and those huge crowds engendered excitement when otherwise (for male football, there is still the AFLW) there would have been the high drama of … a legends’ match. But this year they had Collingwood one night and Carlton the next. Of course they got crowds and TV numbers like that. If next year’s wildcard round is North Melbourne v Gold Coast and GWS v Port Adelaide, and the numbers are barely a fraction of this year’s, will the AFL say “well that didn’t work, look at the crowds”? Blues fans could be forgiven for struggling to believe what they’re seeing. AFL Photos For the team that finishes 10th in a competition of 18 to be rewarded with a chance to play finals remains illogical.

Advertisement

Melbourne, who finished the regular season 10 points – two and a half wins – ahead of Carlton had to play a side that was rewarded for two thirds of a great season. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The Blues never dreamed of coming this far. The Cats are next in their sights The football on Friday night was tense and tight and a cracking game that finished after the siren. But it also had the feel of eighth playing ninth. The argument to counter the idea of a lack of integrity inherent in rewarding mediocre teams is that wildcard is another AFL retrofit to fix other fixturing problems. Maybe it is fair to give a chance to two sides that might have finished outside the old final eight only by virtue of the compromised fixture. Maybe that compromised fixture punished them more than the teams above them with short breaks, cross-country travel (clearly not Collingwood’s reason for finishing ninth), the number of terrible versus terrific teams they played … or coaches they had to sack mid-year.

Advertisement

Wildcard round will continue because it was high drama. The football was thrilling, tight throughout both games, intense, pressured and great theatre. One bloke hit the post four times, the best small forward in the game missed shots he would usually kick, the two best players in the competition went head-to-head and both played well. Carlton and Collingwood are box-office teams, so drama follows them. But when one plays in a game decided after the siren and the other is riding a wave and in-season turnaround unseen in football, then that drama captivates everyone. The wildcard round meant Carlton’s ride was not forced to end this year in Shakespearean (wispy half-back, good on his left, played at the Globe) drama, achingly short of finals. View post on X The greatest gift the wildcard gave was keeping alive the best storyline of the year. No one – save for Melbourne who, were enjoying an extraordinary turnaround under a new coach of their own (and OK probably also a lot of people who just hate Carlton) – wanted to see the Josh Fraser transformation stop here. Now the Blues play Geelong, a team they have beaten the past three times.

Advertisement

Carlton’s story has delivered the AFL the narrative to go with the economics. Friday night was a close, tough game where it felt like Bulldogs should be five goals clear for most of the night, but Craig McRae’s Collingwood have a gift for competing and staying in touch. It ended in a missed shot at goal after the siren. This actually shouldn’t have been a surprise, it was the fourth Collingwood game this year decided by a kick on or after the siren. Related Article AFL 2026 How the Blues are harnessing the energy of their boisterous fans to ‘break’ rivals Football likes to present itself as romantic (there is no other reason to have the father-son rule), but business pragmatism is always more compelling. Without getting into the weeds, romance delivered Tasmania a team, but business delivered Tasmania a roofed-stadium-or-bust ultimatum that was not demanded of either Gold Coast or GWS in the states the AFL’s marketeers coveted. Romance only goes so far. This wildcard round of quasi-finals, or round 25 if you’re Ed Richards, has given the AFL the most perfect weekend it could have hoped for. It doesn’t necessarily make it the right thing for football, but it makes it the concept that is here to say. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. title: Trump’s Venezuela oil deal has seismic potential, but it’s an idea not a reality
text:
Advertisement

Analysis WorldNorth AmericaOil Trump’s Venezuela oil deal has seismic potential, but it’s an idea not a reality Michael Koziol August 30, 2026 — 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: As far as announcements go, it was pretty low-key. Word came from US President Donald Trump’s Truth Social account just before 7pm on Friday, a time slot typically reserved for bad news you want to bury. Instead, Trump unveiled an unprecedented deal for the US to take control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, in what he billed as the largest such agreement in world history. Donald Trump has his sights set on unlocking Venezuela’s oil. Marija Ercegovac “This Historic Transaction MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves, greatly increases our Oil Supply, and will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future, while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity,” he said. There have been no documents to accompany the announcement, and few details – though Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, provided some information.

Advertisement

She said the deal called for the development of 17 strategic oil fields, with proven potential of 65 billion barrels. It would involve an investment of $US100 billion ($140 billion) and it would yield “more than $US209 billion” in tax revenue for Venezuela, she said. Related Article Trump diplomacy Trump says US has agreed to deal with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves With Trump, we are used to brash overselling of achievements and deals. But in this case, the upside for both nations has the capacity to be significant – if it ever comes to fruition. Venezuela is in a parlous state and it was so for many years under the dictatorial socialist regime of Nicolás Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell on trial for drug trafficking (he and his wife have pleaded not guilty). Its ability to harvest the world’s largest proven oil reserves, some 303 billion barrels, was badly compromised, though things have started to turn around since Maduro was captured by US forces and Rodriguez was installed.

Advertisement

The beneficiary has been the United States. At a time when it has had to draw down its Strategic Petroleum Reserves to compensate for the supply shock caused by the war in Iran, the US has dramatically increased oil imports from Venezuela. In December, before Maduro was captured, the US imported 4.26 million barrels of Venezuelan crude oil and petroleum products. By May, that figure had risen to 16.85 million. Venezuela is now the US’s second-largest overseas source of oil, behind only Canada. But to go beyond that will require significant investment from American oil companies, something they have thus far been reluctant to entertain. However, Chevron, the second-largest US oil firm and the only one with a sizeable presence in Venezuela, is in talks to expand its operations. Trump’s deal is aimed at beginning this process. A US official said it gave the US 55 per cent of the effective output from a new private joint venture, split between holding company equity and at-cost offtake for the federal government. The venture will become the second-largest private oil company in the world by reserves, after Saudi Aramco.

Advertisement

Nicolás Maduro was unceremoniously removed from power by the US in a bold military raid in January. NYT “As the company scales production, the resulting stable supply of at-cost oil in our hemisphere will go toward filling the US strategic petroleum reserve and fulfilling the supply needs of our great US military,” the official said. So, this is a long-term play, and it is certainly not one that will lower petrol prices for US motorists now. Enticing billions in investment from US companies also depends on continued stability in Venezuela. To that end, it remains unclear if and when elections will be held in that country. “They’re not really ready for them yet,” Trump said in July. Talks in Venezuela – which the US says it is facilitating, not dictating – are led by Jorge Rodriguez, the brother of Delcy Rodriguez and president of the National Assembly, and former politician Dinorah Figuera, a relatively obscure figure representing the opposition.

Advertisement

Related Article Venezuela crisis Stealth drones and massive blowtorches: How the US mission to capture Maduro unfolded Politico reported on Sunday that the talks were largely taking place at the JW Marriott hotel in central Caracas, which has acted as ground zero for US activity in the capital since Maduro’s removal. American energy company executives “broker deals in the lobby”, according to Politico. Trump made no secret from the outset that gaining access to Venezuela’s enormous oil reserves was a top factor, maybe the overriding one, in his decision to kidnap Maduro at the start of the year. He told reporters he had briefed oil company chiefs in advance and he said they couldn’t wait to go in and start taking the oil. In theory, sure – but in practice, it is still a huge risk. And how will this apparent deal be seen by Venezuelans? After all, it’s an agreement struck between the Trump administration and an interim president who serves with Washington’s imprimatur – not a deal made with any legitimately elected government.

Advertisement

Indeed, it underlines that Trump’s priority is to exploit Venezuela’s oil, not to bring democracy to Caracas. Venezuela has some of the world’s largest proven oil reserves, but unlocking its potential will take huge investment after years of decline. AP Rafael Ramirez, who was energy minister under former Venezuelan president Hugo Chavez, and president of the state-owned oil company PDVSA at the same time, said the deal was “another ambush” by the Americans. “It will go down in history for being a sellout and for opening the doors to the new colonialism of the United States,” he said on X. “An agreement behind the country’s back, clearly unconstitutional, that cedes control of the territory and the oil to a foreign power.” Emmanuel Rincón, a Miami-based political consultant focusing on Latin America, said Trump “has handed the anti-imperialist Latin American left a powerful weapon that they will use to win elections for decades”.

title: Sydney Marathon results 2026: Gobena and Jepchirchir crowned champions as thousands participate in Sydney Marathon
text:
Two years ago, after Raul Carrera tore up his meniscus, doctors told him he would never run again. On Sunday, the Arizona native proved them wrong when he crossed the finish line at the Sydney Marathon.

Slumped over the barricade, tears streaming down his face, Carrera sobbed. “I am here. I did it.”

An emotional Raul Carrera after finishing the Sydney Marathon. Audrey Richardson

“There were times I really wanted to quit,” Carrera said. “I got to Mrs Macquarie’s Chair and thought I wasn’t going to make it, but I just kept putting one foot in front of the other.”

Under a clear azure sky, they came in their thousands, the atmosphere electric. One did not need to be a runner to be swept up in marathon mania. Spectators on the sideline whooped, cheered and whistled to energise the passing throng. Among the runners were famous faces including Olympian Emma McKeon, three-time Grand Slam singles winner Ash Barty and Olympian boxer Harry Garside.

McKeon, a six-time Olympic gold medallist and one of the best freestyle swimmers in Australian history, finished in a time of 4:41:30.

Six-time Olympic gold medal winner Emma McKeon after finishing the Sydney Marathon. Audrey Richardson

After Sydney gained World Marathon Major status, this year, 123,000 people entered the ballot, vying for just 40,000 spots. With no priority given to local runners, thousands missed out. Some showed up anyway.

“You got my ballot spot – enjoy it,” read one sign.

Jenny Tran, who missed out on an entry, ran along the sidelines to cheer on her friend. “It’s so empowering. Everyone is so positive,” she said, adding that she planned to try and sneak onto the track for the final two kilometres.

In the elite field, Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir was crowned the women’s champion, finishing in 02:18:31 to add Sydney to her major victories in Boston, New York and London.

Addisu Gobena wins the Sydney Marathon. Audrey Richardson

In the men’s division, 21-year-old Ethiopian Addisu Gobena – a javelin thrower until 2023 – shattered the course record by almost a minute and a half, crossing the line in 2:04:42.

At the 12km mark, in the shadow of the Cahill Expressway, runners were met with energy shots, blasting music and an emcee amping up the crowd.

“It’s wonderful. It is early, but it feels like the middle of the afternoon,” said spectator Christian Torres from Mexico. “My job is to cheer on my friend and other people. As a runner, it cheers you up a lot and gives you a boost.”

As runners exited the Sydney Harbour Bridge, one woman waved a homemade poster: “Welcome to Sydney. That’ll be $8.50.” Another crowd-pleasing sign spotted in the crowd: “Pain is temporary but Strava is forever.”

Thousands of runners cross the Sydney Harbour Bridge for the marathon. George Chan

For spectators like Nicolas Soares, simply watching the runners was enough to get his heart pumping. “Everything is beautiful. It’s a perfect day for running. Not too hot, not too cold. It’s beautiful”, he said.

The marathon split the city like a river. With roads closed for the steady stream of athletes, pedestrians lined up to be ushered across the track. For a few seconds, they too were part of the marathon.

At the Opera House finish line, best friends Charlotte Forelich and Shannon McIvor wept after completing their first – and last – marathon, propelled through Sydney’s famously punishing hills by what McIvor called “radical delusion”.

“I am in pain,” Forelich said. “It was amazing, but it was mentally very challenging. I think I stopped at 30 kilometres for a little cry, but I’m still here.”

Rosslyne and Michael Wilson have a moment at the finish line. George Chan

Emotions were high for spectators. Rosslyne Wilson, mother of runner Michael Wilson, had tears streaming down her face as her son crossed the finish line.

“He has done an amazing job. He is so hard on himself. He is so brilliant,” she said.

The proud mother told the Herald her son had recently run 100 kilometres around a Bendigo athletics track to raise money for bowel cancer.

Amid the lycra was the occasional costume. Phil Brent, dressed head to toe as a turtle, broke a Guinness World Record for “fastest marathon dressed in a reptile costume”. He had just a single training run in the outfit. “I ran around my local area at nighttime. I didn’t want anyone to see me,” Brent said.

Phil Brent poses with his Sydney Marathon medal and his new world record. Audrey Richardson

Perched on her partner’s shoulders, Central Coast woman Tayla Mackay was on top of the world.

It was the 25-year-old’s second marathon, and she smashed her personal best. Despite being “very sore and very tired”, Mackay was buzzing. “I cried when I saw my mum. I think I’m going to have to do all the world majors now.”

But for now, Mackay was off to a much-awaited destination: the pub.

title: Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed in Argentina
text:

SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed in Argentina Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter August 30, 2026 — 1:37pm

August 30, 2026 — 1:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Wallabies continued their winning ways under new coach Les Kiss, posting their fourth straight win for the first time since 2021. Here’s our rating for each Wallabies player. 1. Isaac Kailea 5.5/10 In his first Test in 630 days, the mobile NSW prop looked to use his feet at the line with early carries. But was one of many to find it hard going against the Pumas’ defence and otherwise had limited involvements in his 40 minutes. Set-piece work was solid. Loading 2. Brandon Paenga-Amosa 7.5

Advertisement

BPA is a good example of how front-rowers age like a good red wine. A Malbec, perhaps. At the age of 30 and with a stint in France under his belt, the former garbo is now in the form of his life on all fronts: lineout throwing, scrummaging, defence, ball carrying and he’s also a consistent try sneak. Effort to be in the left corner to score in Jujuy deserves a toast. 3. Allan Alaalatoa 7 There is a good argument that an eyes-up back such as Ryan Lonergan should be looked as Wallabies captain when Harry Wilson doesn’t play. But then you see Alaalatoa lead like he did against the Pumas, and you understand why he gets the armband. Has a rare combination of calm and menace, and hits like a train. 4. Josh Canham 7.5 Quick reminder this guy was only playing in his seventh Test in Jujuy. It’s easy to overlook, given how much impact Canham brings as an athletic carrier, lineout operator and as one of the most effective ball handlers, as well. Always seems to have an offload ready.

Advertisement

5. Jeremy Williams 7.5 Returned to the starting line-up and turned in another high-quality 80-minute performance. At 113kg, Williams is on the lighter end of the scale for tighthead locks in Test rugby, but the Wallabies’ scrum doesn’t seem to suffer. His mobility and skill pay dividends in open play: see try assist for BPA. Tom Hooper of the Wallabies scores a try. Getty Images 6. Tom Hooper 8 Was always a workhorse but Hooper has become more of an athlete since joining Exeter, and that was shown with an 80-minute effort featuring 14 runs, 11 tackles, two key turnovers and the try that ultimately secured the game. Coming off a long break with a shoulder injury, it was very impressive and combined with the other two below, it makes picking a back row difficult for Les Kiss next week.

Advertisement

7. Fraser McReight 8 McReight has already had a superb year and the headgeared flanker now routinely gets ranked in the world’s top five back-rowers. And fair enough. Yet another all-singing, all-dancing display: one try, 11 carries, team-high 14 tackles and a late steal that denied Argentina a potential win. 8. Rob Valetini 8.5 Rob Valetini gets the ball away in traffic. Getty Images Are we totally sure big Bobby V isn’t part-machine? Back in the starting side after a rest in Townsville, and Valetini turned yet another powerhouse performance: team-high 17 carries and equal team-high tackles (14) with McReight, and a goal line turnover (we’ll forget the kick). Back at his favoured No.8 spot and such a luxury to have a guy who’ll quietly roll his sleeves up every single time he plays.

Advertisement

9. Ryan Lonergan 6.5 Solid effort in the first half, albeit with some missed tackles and a rare shank off the kicking tee. Left the field early in the second half after a head knock when making a try-saving cover tackle, but it was also due to a flu. 10. Carter Gordon 6.5 Nice to see Gordon getting through games and threatening the line with his under-rated running game and his sharp passing. Scored a good try with a hard line. Gordon’s kicking game is a strength, but we haven’t seen it in full flight yet. Short kicking might have been effective against the Pumas’ line speed, too. Carter Gordon of the Wallabies is challenged by Ignacio Mendy and Santiago Carreras. Getty Images

Advertisement

11. Harry Potter 5 A day of limited involvement for Potter on the left wing, with only a handful of runs and mixed results in the aerial contest space. Points off for spending 10 minutes in the sin bin after going for an unwise, low-percentage intercept with one hand. 12. Hunter Paisami 6.5 Plenty of tough carries, including the support run that saw Paisami break through and led to Hooper’s crucial try. Ikitau is every chance to return next week, but this has been an important block for Paisami to prove himself indispensable to Les Kiss’s squad going forward, even after he moves to Japan next year. 13. Isaac Henry 5.5

Advertisement

A quiet day was always going to come for Henry after the high-octane opening two Tests. The ball simply didn’t come his way much, in attack or defence. But nor did he make any major mistakes. Max Jorgensen celebrates after Australia’s win over Argentina. Getty Images 14. Max Jorgensen 7.5 Jorgensen made his name by being an open-field whiz, with incredible feet and deception. But Test rugby doesn’t give you as much space, so the youngster is now providing value in other ways: he is the Wallabies’ best man in the air, he is strong carrying in traffic and he can also muscle up in defence, as seen in Jujuy. 15. Tom Wright 5.5

Advertisement

Another who was solid but not spectacular, with mixed kicking outcomes and some wayward passing. Wright at his best is always threatening around the ball, particularly for the Brumbies, and it’d be good to see him lurking in closer channels for the Wallabies. Reserves 16. Billy Pollard 6.5 Always brings energy and fast leg-speed from the bench, but his massive hit in the last 10 minutes – that preceded McReight’s steal – showed the ex-leaguie still lurking in Pollard. Angus Bell 6.5

Advertisement

17. Solid 40-minue effort from Bell, but didn’t get the ball enough to see any of his trademark wind-up carrying. The Wallabies hung on to beat Argentina to make it four straight wins for the first time since 2021., Getty Images 18. Massimo De Lutiis 6.5 The Reds love big “Mass” for his power in contact, and we saw some of that with plenty of carries and some post-gainline metres, to boot. So far, showing he can handle Test rugby.

Advertisement

19. Lachlan Shaw 5.5 Has a bit of Canham about him in the athleticism, but Shaw is also learning on the job at Test level; he’d take back a loose flick pass in the second half that scuttled one attacking move. 20. Charlie Cale 6 Limited minutes from the bench, but grabbed a couple of pressure lineout wins in the dying stages that helped get Australia home. 21. Tate McDermott 6

Advertisement

Steady performance from the reserve halfback when he replaced Lonergan, but box kicking game is still not his forte, and the only glimpse of McDermott’s lethal running game led to a held-up. 22. Ben Donaldson 5 Almost 20 minutes on the field as a replacement for Gordon and Wright, but a missed conversion for Hooper’s try kept the game tight, and pushing a pass in the dying moments from a line break – that led to a turnover – was also unnecessary. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii throws a no-look pass. Getty Images 23. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii 7 Clearly was out to make an impact with his 15 minutes on the field, and the highly paid recruit did that with four carries and the second-most metres run in the whole team. Looked threatening.

Carlton star Adam Cerra says the Blues are feeding off the energy of their revitalised fans, and has revealed a key plank of coach Josh Fraser’s mantra as they push to continue their September dream and “break” Geelong next weekend. The Blues’ remarkable uprising continued on Saturday night when they ran over Melbourne by 19 points in a high-pressure wildcard clash in front of 91,733 fans at the MCG, booking an elimination final against Geelong at the MCG on Friday. Hear the roar: Star Blue Adam Cerra wants the Blues’ army to come out in force against the Cats on Friday night. Getty Images The deafening roar of the Blues’ fans enthralled by a stunning resurgence under Fraser out-powered their Demons’ rivals, and the Blues want this to continue against the rested Cats. “We play off their [fans’] energy, and we try and energise them through our footy,” Cerra told this masthead.

“We know it’s a strength of this football club; the Carlton community, how big and strong that is, and we try and use it to our advantage. They come out in numbers. Our part is to play an exciting brand of football to energise them, give them a good game of footy to watch. We love doing that.” Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The Blues never dreamed of coming this far. The Cats are next in their sights The Blues have been doing that since Michael Voss was sacked after a 1-8 start to the season, with 12 wins and a draw from their next 15 games, with a simplified, high-possession game plan that rivals have yet to consistently counter. They have also altered their mindset when it comes to crunch time in games. Where they all but froze earlier in the year, they now embrace tight contests, adopting a “just play the minutes” ethos. Cerra, who had 26 disposals across half-back and in the midfield against the Demons, said the Blues wanted to “break” opponents.

“It might take 118 minutes to break a team, but we have full trust. It might not come in the first quarter, but we stick to the process and try and break them by the end,” Cerra said. Cerra delivered insight into the hoodie-wearing Fraser’s mindset of how the Blues handle adversity, including against the Demons when they conceded the opening four goals. Loading “The main messaging since ‘Frase’ has come in is – ‘just play your minutes’. No matter what is going on in the game, we are just going to chase, just play the minutes,” Cerra said. “That’s why I think we are playing that game well now. We are not getting caught up in the scoreboard. We know momentum will come and go.

“Stay present, don’t worry about the external things, the scoreboard, whether we are kicking goals or hitting the post, like [against the Demons in the final term] – we are on to the next thing. “It’s really led by our leaders, first and foremost, who are driving a calm presence across the field to trust that process and trust the work we do through the week.” Fraser has regularly told players and the public the Blues have set high standards at training. A focused, consistent training plan has helped deliver success. “Throughout the week, our standards at training, habits, we try and make every session the best session of the year,” Cerra said.

Advertisement

“That gives us real confidence to go out and play our brand for four quarters. We trust the work we do through the week. It’s really fulfilling when you come and see it come to fruition.” Cerra also praised the maturation of a side focused on defence and role-play. He said star youngsters Jagga Smith and Harry Dean embodied this. The Blues have been purring since Josh Fraser took charge. Chris Hopkins “I think all the young boys, Harry Dean, Talor Byrne, they are just doing the right things. They value the hardest part of the game, defending, putting on pressure. They get the rewards on the back of that,” Cerra said. “Jagga got the rewards on the back of that, another night it might be Talor kicking a few goals. The bottom line is they put on pressure and stay disciplined in their role, and they respect the hardest part of the game. So, it’s pretty rare to have 18-year-olds come in and have that awareness already.”

So is the ownership.” The Blues expect Will Hayward (ankle) to be available for a recall – he booted a team-high three goals in a four-point win over the Cats in round 12. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has taken aim at One Nation after a historic late-night byelection victory by the party in Labor’s stronghold of Western Australia, saying it was crucial to defeat hard-right populists. On Sunday morning, Albanese addressed a crowd of Labor faithful at the party’s annual Queensland conference, hours after One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen claimed the outer suburban seat of Secret Harbour in Perth. Albanese said One Nation leader Pauline Hanson sought to divide Australians, and that she talked Australians down. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (centre) and Treasurer Jim Chalmers (far left) with delegates at the Queensland Labor state conference in Brisbane on Sunday. “They can’t say what their immigration numbers are … they just have no idea when it comes to serious policy development,” he said.

Advertisement

“This is a crucial time for our movement because across the world, hard-right populists are on the march, peddling politics that is dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest. “We simply must defeat them. We owe it to history. We owe it to the nation, and we will defeat them. Anthony Albanese was adamant that Labor must defeat One Nation, declaring “we owe it to history”. “They’ll say anything and do anything, bend any backs, peddle misinformation and disinformation, turn Australian against Australian.” Albanese said One Nation had no serious answers to problems, and the party’s own division and disagreement was beginning to show.

Advertisement

He pointed to when One Nation won 11 seats in Queensland in 1998, they “lost them all in record time”. He questioned how they would work in a coalition with the LNP, saying it was a fact that they had to govern together. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership ‘Treading water’: Albanese pivots to positivity to counter Hanson gloom Albanese spruiked several policies he said had improved the lives of Australians, and told the crowd the only mainstream political force that sought to govern in the interests of the Australian people was the Labor Party. He said the best way to beat the “coalition of chaos” was to give Australians hope, to “stay positive”, and to be a party with ideas that would make people’s lives better. This positivity is a sentiment that has crept into the prime minister’s speeches, in a pivot to respond to a growing sense of pessimism about the nation’s future.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who spoke moments before Albanese, told the crowd the government was aware of the One Nation threat. “We took this threat seriously before yesterday’s byelection in the west, and we will take it seriously after it,” Chalmers said. He said Australia, its cohesion, its people, and the economy were under threat by a dangerous and divisive coalition of chaos – “a three-ring circus of Liberals, Nationals and One Nation, with that karaoke clown from Melbourne [Liberal treasury spokesman Tim Wilson] as its chief economic spokesman”. Queensland Opposition Leader Steven Miles told the two-day conference on Saturday that the next election would be a fight between Labor and a far-right coalition of the LNP and One Nation. William Davis “Today, the biggest fault lines in our politics aren’t just between the centre left and the extreme right, but between those of us who want to address and alleviate the legitimate frustrations that people feel about the cost of living and other pressures, and those who just want to pick at them and prey on them,” he said.

On Saturday, Queensland Opposition Leader Steven Miles took aim at the Crisafulli LNP government, arguing it would need to form a coalition with One Nation to retain government at the next election. “If you think they’re bad now, imagine what they would be like in coalition with One Nation, because the next election will be a fight between Labor and a far-right coalition of the LNP and One Nation swapping preferences and hoping to govern together,” he told the crowd. Miles also confirmed that frontbencher and possible future leader Meaghan Scanlon would recontest the seat of Gaven, after speculation she may be moved to a safer district. title: ‘Miraculous’: Joy for Aussie hiker’s parents
text:
The parents of a young Australian woman who had been missing after the Nepal flooding catastrophe say they are "elated" after she was found safe and well, as the number of Australians unaccounted for grew to 42.

In a statement, Cara Severino's parents Debbie and Frank thanked the Australian consul staff for finding her, while offering prayers for the thousands caught up in the disaster.

"Seeing Cara's name appear on my message bank, hearing her voice and now seeing her photo and speaking with her has been the most miraculous gift," they said in statement.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We are incredibly thankful to the Australian Consular Response teams for locating her bringing her to safety and for the care they are giving her and all the amazing work they are doing to locate others.

"We are so grateful to her Nepalese hiking partners who saw her through a harrowing several days of hiking in very difficult terrain, so thankful that they have all made it to safety.

"The scale of this tragedy is staggering and amidst our personal joy we continue to stand in prayer with the many families here in Australia, in Nepal and around the world who have lost loved ones or are still waiting to hear from them, we know that the waiting is horrendous."

Cara Severino, 26, made contact with her parents after being feared missing the Nepal floods. Picture: Instagram

DevGhat village in Nepal was devastated after the flash flood on August 28, leaving thousands unaccounted for. Picture: Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images

They said the return of Cara had been a "miracle".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We are beyond relieved and so elated to have Cara safe and well and we can't wait to hold her in our loving arms," they said.

"This morning we are being enfolded in love by our church family who, along with so many of our family and friends, have been praying with us for this miracle. We thank Jesus for answering these prayers.

Aussie hiker survives

Ms Severino was among dozens of Australians caught up in the incident, and was unaccounted for several days before she was able to make contact with embassy officials on Saturday.

Ms Severino, who remains the only Australian to have been located, said she got out safely thanks to the "amazing people" she had been with at a national park when the disaster unfolded.

Cara Severino (third from left) after she survived the deadly flash floods in Nepal. Picture: DFAT

Ms Severino made contact with her parents after being feared missing the Nepal floods. Picture: Instagram

The 26-year-old was hiking in the region and is now safe in Kathmandu. Picture: Instagram

She recounted a devastating story of locals who were unable to escape the devastation.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We passed a guy hiking up to Thulu Safru who lost his whole family when their whole town was destroyed. It's just so devastating and undeserving," she said.

"I feel for the families of those still missing, I know how much my family and friends went through.

"Blessed to be from Australia and have the embassy and Australian government giving so much support."

Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed the news on Saturday afternoon.

"This is a rare piece of positive news amid a disaster that has brought immense loss and uncertainty," Senator Wong said.

She said officials were transporting Ms Severino to a safe location and continue to monitor her condition.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Thistlethwaite also welcomed the news and the efforts of Australian consular staff.

"So, it's one of the, unfortunately few good news stories from this terrible tragedy," he said

On Sunday morning, Nepalese officials said they were still monitoring a large dam which had formed along a segment of valley, creating potential for more flooding in the area.

Dozens of Australians are still unaccounted for. Picture: Nepal Police

DFAT has sent officials to assist in locating Australians as the recovery begins. Picture: DFAT

Albanese mourns disaster in 'awesome' region

Anthony Albanese on Sunday took time during a speech to the Queensland state Labor conference to reflect on "the tragedy in Nepal that has resulted in such devastation and loss of life", including potentially many Australians.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Our thoughts and prayers are with their families and friends, with the people of Nepal, and with the citizens of every country caught up in this calamity," the Prime Minister said.

"Our hope is that many of those missing are found alive.

"That something so devastating could occur in such an awesome and inspiring corner of the world during times of pilgrimage and holiday makes the blow seem even more heartbreaking."

He said Australia was responding with significant consular, rescue and humanitarian aid.

42 Aussies still missing

Earlier on Sunday morning, Assistant Foreign Minister Matt Thistlethwaite confirmed the number of Aussies still missing had grown.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"So, it's one of the, unfortunately few good news stories from this terrible tragedy," he said, while confirming that 42 other Australians were now unaccounted for.

"Unfortunately, the number has risen to 42 today based on the advice from the Nepalese Tourism Board and our officials on the ground," he said.

"We haven't given up hope. Our officials are working around the clock to try and locate those missing Australians and hopefully return them home safely to their families."

More than 3000 people are still missing, while the number of people confirmed dead is nearing 700.

More than 3000 people are still missing days after the devastating flash flood. Picture: NewsWire Handout/ World Vision

Mr Thistlethwaite said the latest figures indicate a total of 6633 people had been rescued, including 261 foreigners.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"(It) is a remarkable effort and we haven't given up hope, given that those figures rise every day," he said.

"Yesterday it was 121 foreigners had been rescued. So, it's more than doubled in the course of 24 hours."

On Wednesday, a huge chunk of ice broke off a glacier high up in the mountains along the Nepalese-Tibetan border, sending a wave of mud, water and rock cascading down through the heavily populated valleys below.

Glacier expert's dire warning

University of Tasmania glaciologist Poul Christopherson said "ice avalanches" like this one were becoming more frequent, even in mountainous terrain which is supposed to stay cold all year round.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We see these ice avalanches more frequently now, even in mountainous terrain. Despite such high altitudes, it still gets warm in summer," he said.

Flood-affected communities in Rasuwa are facing significant damage to homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods. Picture: NewsWire Handout/ World Vision

Professor Christopherson said when the ice fell, it was pulverised, turning into "fragments and blocks of ice and dirt" which travelled down the valley and turned into "a destructive sludge".

"This could have been triggered by a landslip underneath the glacier because it's on such steep terrain and mountainous terrain, but it could have also been because the ice itself has warmed over time and not been able to stay attached in such steep terrain."

Professor Christopherson said Nepal wasn't the only part of the world where ice falls from glaciers were becoming a genuine safety risk.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"There is real concern in mountain communities about these natural disasters which are associated with both ice and ice avalanches, but also rock slope instability and mountainsides becoming unstable," he said.

Professor Christopherson said mountain and valley communities will be forced to deal with these kinds of events more frequently in the future. Picture: NewsWire Handout/ World Vision

"I have studied glaciers above the town of Chamonix in France, and some of the glacier sites where tourists used to go have now been sealed off. You can't access them anymore because they have been deemed too dangerous.

"This is another example of a terrible incident where we need to reflect on what's happening and the underlying causes.

"It's easy to sometimes dispel climate change as not being significant when you hear that we are reaching up to 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial times, but this is what can happen."
